title: Once props
description: Remember expensive values on the client and skip them on later visits.
body: Use once props for expensive values that rarely change. The client remembers a once prop across visits. It tells the server which keys it holds with X-Inertia-Except-Once-Props , so the server can skip them on later visits. Behavior - The value is left out on later visits, but the onceProps entry stays so the client keeps its copy. - .Fresh() sends the value even when the client has it. - Partial reloads always resolve once props that the reload asks for. - Expiry is computed from the registered TimeProvider , so tests can use FakeTimeProvider . - .As(key) and .Until(ttl) imply once. - Sharing a key between pages lets the client reuse one value across them. Keys The default key is the prop path. Use .As("billing-plans") when the same value is exposed under different names, or when you want a stable key across page changes. Two props that share a key are treated as the same client value. Only share a key when the values are the same. If you are not sure, use the default prop path. Expiry .Until(TimeSpan) sets expiresAt in milliseconds since the Unix epoch. The client stops treating the key as loaded after that time and requests the value again. The server leaves the value out only when the client lists the key in X-Inertia-Except-Once-Props . Shared once props A shared once prop is the equivalent of Laravel's shareOnce . The client keeps the value across visits. Testing InertiaPage.OnceProps exposes the metadata: Revisit the page with the same client and assert that the prop is missing while onceProps remains.

title: Build a todo app
description: Build ForgetMeNot step by step with shadcn/ui, covering sign-in, shared lists, infinite scroll, live reminders and server-side rendering, using named routes, typed routes and caching.
headings: 2. Make it look good with shadcn/ui
7. Share a list, and render it on the server
8. A reminder that appears by itself
body: ForgetMeNot is a small todo app. It is small, but it uses the same pieces as a real product: - sign-in - private data - a public page - a long list that loads as you scroll - a reminder that appears on your screen without a refresh Each step tells you what to do and why . If you know why a line is there, you can change it later with confidence. - The .NET 10 or .NET 11 SDK - Bun, npm, pnpm or Yarn. The commands on this page use Bun. If you use another tool, use it in place of Bun. - A code editor and a terminal You do not need a database server. The app uses SQLite, a database that lives in one file. What you will build Each feature in this table shows one idea from Inertia.Net. The right column names the idea. You build You learn --- --- A polished interface shadcn/ui cards, lists, switches and a theme you can change in one place Sign in with a cookie The --auth starter, redirects to the login page, and a sign-in rate limit A page of lists Page records, named routes and the typed routes.ts file A form that checks itself Precognition: the server validates a field as you type Slow numbers that load after the page Deferred props, plus a cache you clear when data changes A list with thousands of items ToPageAsync and infinite scroll A link anyone can open Server-side rendering and the SSR cache A reminder that shows up by itself Live props over SignalR Tests Inertia.Net.Testing 1. Create the app Install the templates once, then create the app. The --auth option adds cookie sign-in, so you do not write that yourself. For the other clients, use --framework vue or --framework svelte . Then pick the matching tab in the examples below. Start the two development processes and keep both terminals open: Open http://localhost:5180 , click Log in , and sign in with demo@example.com and the password password . Try the pages before you change anything. Vite serves your React, Vue or Svelte code and reloads it when you save. ASP.NET Core serves the pages. While Vite runs, it writes a small file called wwwroot/hot . The app reads this file to find Vite. You do not need to set up anything else. The template is not empty. It already uses the features this tutorial needs. This table shows where they are: Where What it does Why it matters --- --- --- HomePage , LoginPage in Program.cs Page records. A record that names its component once: Component = "Home" The props and the page name stay together, and the compiler checks them .WithName("login") on each route Named routes The name stays the same when the URL changes. You can change the URL and nothing breaks ClientApp/types/routes.ts Typed routes , written from the names In the browser you write routes.login() , never the string "/login" ClientApp/types/inertia.d.ts TypeScript types for every page, written from the C records A renamed property is a compile error, not a blank spot on the page .WithInertiaPrecognition() on the login The form checks a field on the server when you leave it One set of rules, run in the browser and on the server AddInertiaErrorPages() A 404 or 500 shows your Error page Visitors never see a raw error The app rewrites both generated files, ClientApp/types/routes.ts and ClientApp/types/inertia.d.ts , when it starts in Development. Never edit them by hand. 2. Make it look good with shadcn/ui The template's pages have almost no styling. This step adds shadcn/ui , a set of components: cards, inputs, checkboxes, switches, lists and more. The components are built on Tailwind CSS. They are copied into your project , so you own the code and can change any of it. First, add Tailwind CSS and an @ shortcut for imports. With the shortcut, you write @/components/ui/button instead of ../../components/ui/button . Start by installing Tailwind CSS: In vite.config.ts , add the Tailwind plugin and the alias. Everything else stays as it is: In tsconfig.json , add this inside compilerOptions , so TypeScript understands the same shortcut: Create ClientApp/app.css with one line. Then import it at the top of the client entry file. The client entry file is ClientApp/app.tsx for React, and ClientApp/app.ts for Vue and Svelte: Now run the shadcn setup and add the components this app needs. The flags answer the setup questions in advance. The nova preset is a clean neutral look. If you leave the flags out, the tool asks you the questions instead. The Svelte tool asks before it changes app.css . Answer yes. Look in ClientApp/components/ui . Those files are yours now. Open button and you see ordinary code, not a library. A library that does almost what you want is hard to change. These components are plain files in your repo. To make a button rounder, edit its file. There is no version to upgrade and nothing hidden. You rarely need to edit a file, though. Theming , in the next section, changes the look of every component at once. Make the theme yours Every shadcn component reads a few CSS variables, such as --primary for the main color. Add this to the end of ClientApp/app.css , and every button, switch and progress bar turns violet with rounder corners: Try other values to see how much one line changes. The .dark block applies when the root element of the page has the dark class. This tutorial does not add a switch for it, but the theme is ready for one. The login page The template's login page is plain HTML, and Tailwind removes the default styles of plain HTML. Replace the login page with a card. A Field groups a label, an input and its error message. The error then appears in the right place, and screen readers announce it. The form still uses withPrecognition . When you leave a field, the server checks that field with the same rules as the real submit. Open http://localhost:5180/login to see the new look. 3. Add a database Lists and items must survive a restart, so the app needs a database. This tutorial uses EF Core with SQLite . EF Core is the usual way to use a database from C , and SQLite needs no server. Install the two packages: Use --version "11. " for the SQLite package. The EF Core version must match your .NET version. Create Data.cs . Its classes are the database shape . They are not what the browser sees. Step 4 covers that. A few choices are worth explaining: - OwnerEmail instead of a users table. The template's demo user already has an email in the sign-in cookie. Using that email as the owner key keeps this guide short. In a real app you would use ASP.NET Core Identity and a user id. - ShareSlug is null until you share. A random secret in the URL is the only thing that opens a public list. There is nothing to guess. When you turn sharing off, the app removes the secret. - RemindedAt makes reminders safe to repeat. If the app restarts halfway through, a reminder that was already sent is never sent twice. - DateTime , not DateTimeOffset , for reminders. SQLite cannot compare DateTimeOffset values inside a query. The app stores UTC times as plain DateTime , so the query RemindAt () line - the /todos endpoints (the ones named todos.index , todos.store , todos.toggle and todos.destroy ) - the /dashboard endpoint and the DashboardPage record - the Todo , TodoStats , TodosPage , NewTodo and TodoStore types - their lines in AppJsonContext at the bottom Then register the database in Program.cs , where the other services are registered: Then create the tables right after var app = builder.Build(); : Production and tests need a different database than your laptop. With GetConnectionString("Default") , they can set ConnectionStrings:Default without a code change. The tests in this tutorial use this. EnsureCreated() builds the tables on the first run. It cannot change them later. When the model changes in a real app, switch to EF Core migrations. 4. Decide what the browser sees Never send a database entity to the browser. An entity may have columns you did not mean to share, such as OwnerEmail . Every change to the table would also change your page. Instead, send small records that hold only what a page needs. Create Models.cs : Three things here are easy to miss: - Form classes are public . The validation generator, AddValidation() , skips internal types. With a private form class, the [Required] rules do nothing, and you get no error. - Events.RemindersChanged(email) is one value used twice. The page uses it to say "refresh me when this happens", and the worker uses it to say "this happened". Because both use the same value, the page and the worker always agree. - Email() hides one claim lookup. Every endpoint asks the same question, "whose list is this?", so the code asks it in one place. The template turned off reflection-based JSON. This keeps the app ready for Native AOT. In return, you must list every type that goes to or from the browser. Add these lines to AppJsonContext at the bottom of Program.cs : Each page record gets its own line when you create it: ListsPage in step 5, ListPage in step 6 and PublicPage in step 7. If you forget a type, you get an error the first time the app sends that type. The message names the type. Add the type to AppJsonContext and try again. 5. The lists page A page record holds the props of a page, which are the values the server sends to the page component. It also holds the code that fills them. Create ListsPage.cs : Add [JsonSerializable(typeof(ListsPage))] to AppJsonContext , then read the handler from top to bottom: 1. The query reads lists straight from the database into ListCard records. AsNoTracking() tells EF Core that the code will not change these rows, which makes the query cheaper. 2. Stats is deferred . The server sends the page right away, and the browser asks for the numbers a moment later. The visitor sees the page sooner, even if counting is slow. 3. .Cache(...) keeps the finished stats for five minutes, so a second visit does not count again. The tags give you a way to clear the cached stats. Every write removes the tag user:email , so the numbers are never wrong for long. 4. Reminders is deferred and live . Step 8 explains it. Now add the routes. Create Endpoints.cs : Call the new method from Program.cs , in the place where the /dashboard endpoint was: Also send people to their lists after they sign in. In the /login endpoint, change the last "/dashboard" to "/lists" . .WithName("lists.store") costs nothing and gives you two things. First, the name becomes routes.lists.store() in your frontend, so you never type "/lists" again. Second, the form's type, RouteBodies['lists.store'] , comes from the C class NewList , so the C and the TypeScript cannot disagree. .WithInertiaPrecognition() does two jobs. First, it sends a normal submit with bad data back to the form with the error messages. Second, the page can ask "is this one field valid?" while the person is still typing, and the server answers without running your code. You write the rules once, on the class, with [Required] and [StringLength] . Make the frontend ready Write the types file and the routes file now. The app does this by itself when it starts in Development. This command does it when you ask, which is useful in CI: Open ClientApp/types/routes.ts . It contains functions you did not write, one for each named route: Now run the build, which also checks the types. It should fail, and that is expected: You deleted the todos and dashboard routes, so TypeScript lists every place that still uses them: the layout and the home page. A URL written as a string would fail without an error, in front of a visitor. A typed route fails during development, where you see it. Fix them one by one. Start with the layout, which every page uses. It has the top bar with the My lists link and the Log out button. It also has an Alert for the flash messages, which are the messages the server sends after an action: Then fix the home page. Its link pointed at the deleted todos route: Finally delete ClientApp/pages/Todos and the Dashboard page ( Dashboard.tsx , Dashboard.vue or Dashboard.svelte ). Run bun run build again. It passes. dotnet build prints INERTIA002 for ListsPage : "this component has no file under ClientApp/pages ". The warning exists to catch a typo, or a page you forgot to write. It goes away in the next step, when you add the page. 6. One list, with infinite scroll A list can have thousands of items. Sending them all would make the page slow. Instead, the server sends one page of items. The browser asks for the next page when the reader scrolls to the end. Create ListPage.cs , and add [JsonSerializable(typeof(ListPage))] to AppJsonContext : - .ToPageAsync(request) comes from Inertia.Net.EntityFrameworkCore . It adds Skip and Take for you and counts the rows. PageRequest reads ?page=2 from the URL by itself. - The order must be unique. The query sorts by IsDone and then by Id . If two items could tie, a row might appear on two pages or on none. - Scroll(items) tells the browser that this value is a list that grows. New pages are merged into items.data instead of replacing it. - Someone else's list is a 404. The query asks for the id and the owner together. The response does not reveal that the list exists. - links.GetPathByName("public.show", ...) is a named route used on the server . The page needs the public address, and the name builds it, so the URL pattern is written in one place only. You add the route in step 7. Until then, the address is empty. Add the rest of the routes to Endpoints.cs , inside MapForgetMeNot , after the two list routes. Also add using System.Security.Cryptography; at the top of the file: Notice the pattern. Each write does the same things in the same order: 1. It checks the owner in the query . 2. It saves . 3. It clears the stats cache . 4. It sends the person back with Back(...) . Back returns the person to the page they came from, so the page shows the new state. WithFlash carries the one-time message. GET /lists/5 is protected, but PATCH /items/9 is a separate endpoint and needs its own check. Every endpoint that takes an id must check that the id belongs to the signed-in person. A missing owner check is the most common security bug in apps like this one. Sharing works like this. The first press of the share button creates a random secret. The second press removes it. Eight random bytes are 16 characters that nobody can guess. Do not use Random or a counter for a secret. Run bun run types again, so the browser knows the new routes and pages. Then add the two pages. First, the lists page. useForm holds the form's values. withPrecognition adds validate to the form, and validate asks the server about one field: Next, the page for one list. Look at InfiniteScroll . It wraps your rows and does the loading for you. Try it: 1. Open My lists and click Add with the box empty. The server answers with "The Title field is required". 2. Paste a title longer than 80 characters and click outside the box. The error appears before you submit. That is Precognition. The message is the same one the server would send. 3. Add a list, add a few items, tick one off and add a reminder. The numbers at the top change, because every write cleared the cached stats. - needs a fallback , even an empty one, or the page will not render. For the stats we show skeleton cards. For the reminders we show nothing until they arrive. - A change reloads the list from the first page. When you tick an item, the server sends the list again, so the extra pages you loaded by scrolling are dropped. That is the cost of the simple Back() redirect. If it matters for your app, reload only what changed with a partial reload. shadcn-svelte's Button is type="button" by default, so inside a form it does nothing. That is why the Svelte pages write type="submit" on their Add buttons. The React and Vue buttons submit by default. 7. Share a list, and render it on the server A shared list is a page that anyone can open, and many people may open the same one. That makes it a good page for server-side rendering (SSR) . Without SSR, the server sends an empty page. The browser has to download JavaScript, run it, and only then show the list. With SSR, the server runs your component first and sends finished HTML. Search engines and slow phones get the content at once. The browser then makes the page interactive with the same code. The share button already exists, from step 6. Only the page it points to is missing. Create PublicPage.cs , add [JsonSerializable(typeof(PublicPage))] to AppJsonContext , and map the route. The route goes in Endpoints.cs : This is the page record, in PublicPage.cs : Look at the last line. .WithSsrCache(...) is the SSR cache . Rendering takes time, and this page looks the same for everyone, so the app can reuse the finished HTML: - For 5 minutes , the app serves the saved HTML without calling the SSR server at all. - For one hour more , the app still serves the saved HTML and makes a new render in the background ( staleFor ). Nobody waits. - The cache key is built from the page's JSON , which includes the title and the items. If the list changes, the JSON changes, the key changes, and the old render is never used. You cannot show a stale page by mistake. A page with per-person props makes one cache entry per person. That wastes memory and gains nothing. The list pages in this app are not cached for that reason. The public page is cached. Turn SSR on. In AddInertia(...) in Program.cs , add: UseNodeProcess makes the app start and watch the SSR process for you. If the SSR process stops answering, the app restarts it. While the SSR process is down, the pages are rendered in the browser instead. Use n.Executable = "node" if you do not have Bun. The SSR process listens on port 13714. If a second Inertia.Net app on the same machine tries to start its own SSR process, that process cannot start. The second app then renders in the browser instead, without an error. You see a warning in the log. To avoid this, give each app its own port: 1. Set the port in C : o.Ssr.UseNodeProcess(n = { n.Executable = "bun"; n.BasePort = 13715; }) . 2. Set the same port in the inertia({ ssr: { port: ... } }) line of vite.config.ts . 3. Run the build again. The port is written into the SSR bundle when the bundle is built, so changing only the C side does not work. We ran two apps side by side this way and both rendered on the server. The SSR bundle needs an entry file and a build setting. The entry file has two lines: In vite.config.ts , tell the Inertia plugin where the entry file is. Also build the SSR bundle into the ssr folder with its dependencies included, so the bundle runs without node modules : Change the build script in package.json so it builds both bundles: Instead of tsc --noEmit , use vue-tsc --noEmit for Vue or svelte-check --tsgo --tsconfig ./tsconfig.json for Svelte. The template's script already has the right command. Only add the last part. Then add the public page: During SSR, the code in a page runs in Node or Bun, where there is no window or document . That is why Show uses a relative link and not window.location.origin . If a component must use the browser, do that inside an effect, which runs only in the browser. To see SSR work, build the app, start it in the Production setting, and look at the page source of a shared list. The list title and the items are there as real HTML: While Vite runs in development, Vite does the rendering itself and the SSR cache is switched off, so every change shows at once. That is why you build and run in Production to see the real behavior. 8. A reminder that appears by itself You can add a reminder time to an item. When the time comes, the My lists page should show the reminder, without anyone reloading. Two parts make that work: a worker that notices due reminders, and a live prop that refreshes the page when it is told to. Start with the worker. A BackgroundService runs for as long as the app runs: - Every 20 seconds is enough for a demo. A real app might use a minute. - CreateScope() gives the worker its own AppDb . The worker runs for as long as the app runs, but a database context must not live that long. - Save first, publish second. The worker marks the reminders as sent before it tells anyone. If the app stops between the two steps, nobody gets the same reminder twice. - try / catch around the work. If one round fails, the worker logs the error and tries again next time. It does not stop. Now look at the line that connects the worker to the page. In ListsPage , you wrote .Live(Events.RemindersChanged(email)) . When the worker publishes that event, the browser reloads only the reminders prop. Nothing else on the page changes. Install the SignalR transport. It carries the "something changed" message to the browser: In Program.cs , register the SignalR transport and the worker, and map the connection endpoint: Without it, nobody can join a private channel. With it, a person can join only the channel named after their own email. Without this check, anyone could listen to anyone's reminders. Keep the rule tight. Finally, turn the client side on. The template already includes ClientApp/lib/inertia-signalr.ts . Import it in the client entry ( app.tsx or app.ts ) and pass it to createInertiaApp : Run the app. Add an item with a reminder one minute from now, open My lists and wait. When the time comes, the reminder appears without a reload. Open the browser's network tab to see how little happens: one small request, only for reminders . Polling asks "anything new?" every few seconds, for every open page, all day. A live prop sends nothing until something changes, and then sends one small request. A live prop is cheaper for the server and faster for the person. A SignalR message reaches only the browsers connected to the server that sent it. Each server would also run its own worker. Behind a load balancer, do these things: - Add a Redis backplane. - Keep the props cache in Redis (see Redis cache). - Run the worker on one instance. For a single server, the setup you have now is correct. 9. Test the important paths The app has a few rules it must never break: - Nobody reads another person's list. - A private list has no public page. - The dashboard's slow numbers arrive after the page. Tests make sure these rules stay true. Create a test project next to the app. Make sure its TargetFramework matches the app's: The test project starts your real app in memory. For that to work, add one line at the very end of the app's Program.cs : Delete the generated UnitTest1.cs and create ListTests.cs : Read the setup, because it explains most of the rest: - A fresh database file per test class. Tests must not see each other's lists. - o.Version = "test" fixes the asset version, so requests do not need a first visit to learn it. - SsrMode.Disabled means the tests do not start Bun. - AllowAutoRedirect = false lets a test look at the redirect itself, such as "a signed-out visitor is sent to /login ". - HandleCookies = true keeps the sign-in cookie and the anti-forgery cookie between requests, like a browser. Run the tests: The template protects every form against cross-site request forgery (CSRF). A real browser gets a cookie and sends it back as a header. In a test, WithXsrfToken copies the token from a page response into your request, so the server accepts the request. If a test fails with a 400, a missing token is usually the reason. 10. Run it in production Build both bundles and publish: Before the app is public, go through this short list. Each item has a reason. Do this Why --- --- Install Bun (or set Executable = "node" ) where the app runs The app starts the SSR bundle with it Keep the Data Protection keys somewhere that survives a restart The sign-in cookie is encrypted with them. A new key signs everyone out Use EF Core migrations instead of EnsureCreated() The tables will change, and EnsureCreated() cannot change them Set ConnectionStrings Default for the real database The file next to the app is only for your laptop Forward the proxy headers when you run behind one The sign-in rate limit counts clients by address. Without the headers, every client looks like the proxy. See Deploying behind a proxy Run one instance, or add Redis for the caches and SignalR The props cache, SSR cache and live messages are per server unless you share them Container examples are in Deploying behind a proxy and the server-side rendering guide. For the container's memory, use the memory table. If something does not build Compare your Program.cs with the finished one: Where to go next You used page records, named and typed routes, Precognition, deferred and cached props, ToPageAsync , infinite scroll, server-side rendering with its cache, live props and the testing helpers. These are the next ones to try: - Once props: remember a value that never changes on the client, such as a list of countries. - Merging props and Partial reloads: update part of a page without replacing it. - Redis cache: share the props and SSR caches between servers. - Authentication: replace the demo user with ASP.NET Core Identity. - Native AOT: a much smaller and faster-starting app, once you avoid EF Core. - Performance: what each feature costs, measured.

title: Quick start
description: Add Inertia.Net to an ASP.NET Core app, create the root template and render your first page.
body: Use this guide to add Inertia to an existing ASP.NET Core app. To create a new app with the server and frontend already connected, follow First 10 minutes. Run these commands from the folder of your existing server project. Every app needs the core package: For MVC, also install Inertia.Net.Mvc . For FastEndpoints, install Inertia.Net.FastEndpoints . Use version 1.9.8 for each. You also need Node.js and Vite to build the client. See installation for all packages, or client setup for the frontend files. The root template is your HTML shell. A page component is the React, Vue or Svelte file that renders a screen. Props are the named values your C handler passes to that component. Every app needs the same four things: 1. Register the services Choose one backend style. All three use the same protocol middleware and the same Render(...) result. AddValidation() enables the Minimal API integration used by .WithInertiaValidation() . UseInertiaAntiforgery() issues the XSRF-TOKEN cookie and validates every unsafe request. This means forms work from the start. See Precognition for live form validation. 2. Add the root template The root template is an HTML file in the content root. The default name is app.html . For Vue and Svelte, remove @viteReactRefresh and point @vite at ClientApp/app.ts . The @inertia token is required. Pages and responses describes the other tokens. Make sure the build copies app.html to the output directory and the publish directory: 3. Create the page component The page name you pass to Render must match the client resolver, which finds the page component for a name. With @inertiajs/vite , the resolver maps ClientApp/pages/ automatically. The client entry only needs to start Inertia: Pass your own resolve and setup functions to createInertiaApp . The client setup page shows both forms for React, Vue and Svelte. 4. Run it If your app has no Vite setup yet, follow the package and configuration steps in Client setup. Use ClientApp/app.tsx (React) or ClientApp/app.ts (Vue and Svelte) as the Vite entry to match the root template above. For the createInertiaApp() examples above, add @inertiajs/vite@^3 as a development dependency. In vite.config.ts , import inertia from @inertiajs/vite and add inertia() after your framework plugin in the plugins array. The inertia() plugin resolves the page files under ClientApp/pages . From the project directory, install dependencies and start Vite with your package manager: Package manager Install dependencies Start Vite Build assets --- --- --- --- npm npm install npm run dev npm run build Bun bun install bun run dev bun run build pnpm pnpm install pnpm run dev pnpm run build Yarn yarn install yarn run dev yarn run build Keep Vite running in terminal 1. Start ASP.NET Core in terminal 2: Open the URL that dotnet watch prints, not the Vite URL. The first visit to / should display “Hello from .NET”. For production, run the build command from your row of the table, then publish the app: Deploy wwwroot/build and app.html with the published app. Where to go next Vite configuration and the React, Vue and Svelte entries. Lazy, deferred, merged and cached page data. Redirects, error bags and Precognition. Render the first visit on Node.

title: Client setup
description: Configure Vite and the React, Vue or Svelte client for an Inertia.Net app.
body: Inertia.Net uses the Inertia.js v3 protocol. Install a v3 client package. Inertia.Net does not support v2 clients. Install the client Run the client setup commands from the ASP.NET Core project directory, the one that contains your .csproj . You can use npm, Bun, pnpm or Yarn. The framework snippets below use npm commands. For another package manager, replace each command with its equivalent: Package manager Add packages Add development packages --- --- --- npm npm install npm install -D Bun bun add bun add -D pnpm pnpm add pnpm add -D Yarn yarn add yarn add -D Replace with the names and version ranges from your framework's snippet. If the project has no package.json , create one first with npm init -y , bun init -y , pnpm init or yarn init . @types/node provides the types for the node:fs import and for process in the Vite config. Add vite/client to tsconfig.json so that import.meta.glob is typed: For Vue and Svelte, use "jsx": "preserve" or omit that setting. The starter templates use ClientApp/pages . The manual examples below use resources/js/Pages . Keep the resolver, file paths and Vite entry consistent with the layout you choose. The templates also ship ClientApp/lib/inertia-signalr.ts , the client transport for live props over SignalR. To turn the transport on, uncomment live: signalr() in ClientApp/app.tsx (or app.ts ). Vite configuration The Vite config is the same for every client, except for the framework plugin and the entry file. The entry file is app.tsx for React and app.ts for Vue and Svelte. Add these fields to package.json : Pass the manifest key of the entry to @vite("...") . The key is resources/js/app.tsx for React and resources/js/app.ts for Vue and Svelte. Client entry The optional @inertiajs/vite plugin resolves pages and mounts the app for you. With the plugin, the client entry file needs only this: Without the plugin, you provide the resolver and the setup function yourself. Pages A page file receives the props from Render(...) as normal component props. Inertia.Net can write TypeScript declarations for your page props, shared props and flash data. See TypeScript types. Development workflow Run Vite in one terminal and the app in a second terminal: Open the ASP.NET Core URL, not the Vite URL. Two servers run side by side: URL What it is Open it? --- --- --- http://localhost:5180 (the template's default) Your app. ASP.NET Core routes the request, runs your endpoint and renders the Inertia page. Yes http://localhost:5173 The Vite dev server. It only serves JavaScript, CSS and hot-reload updates to the page above. No. It has no pages, so it shows a blank page. Vite prints localhost:5173 prominently when it starts. That address is for the browser's asset requests, not for you to open. In Development the app reads wwwroot/hot and renders the Vite tags. In production the app reads the manifest. For production: You need Node to build the assets. At runtime, you need Node only when server-side rendering (SSR) is enabled. Using @inertiajs/vite The @inertiajs/vite plugin also provides the SSR dev endpoint and page resolution. In vite.config.ts , add it before the hot-file plugin: Keep the SSR listener on the loopback address ( 127.0.0.1 ). The renderer trusts its output and has no authentication. The SSR guide covers the full setup.

title: Precognition
description: Validate a form before submission without running its handler.
body: Precognition validates a form before the user submits it. The client sends the same POST as the form, with a Precognition: true header. The server validates the request and returns without running the handler. The Minimal API React sample includes a login validation demo. The demo accepts dummy values and does not create an authentication session. A request and response look like this: The message is the first returned error. A valid request returns 204 and Precognition-Success: true . For Minimal APIs, register AddValidation() and map the endpoint like this: The sample's input model is: Import System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations . .WithInertiaPrecognition() replaces .WithInertiaValidation() . Do not use both. .WithInertiaPrecognition() also handles normal validation redirects. Filters added after it do not run on precognitive requests. A precognitive request is a validation request that carries Precognition: true . FastEndpoints enables Precognition through c.ConfigureInertia() . MVC does not support Precognition. Client setup Inertia 3 includes Precognition in its form integration. Each example validates on blur and displays the error: Precognition-Validate-Only selects which errors the server returns, by field. Nested paths work too. A precognitive request still runs the validator, so keep database rules cheap. Validate on blur for login and payment forms. This avoids showing an error while the user is still typing. setValidationTimeout(3000) raises the debounce interval for expensive rules. It is not the HTTP deadline. Antiforgery and authorization UseInertiaAntiforgery() validates precognitive POSTs like other unsafe requests. The Inertia client sends the token automatically. Authorization middleware runs before endpoint filters, so protected forms validate only for authorized users. Rate limiting Precognitive POSTs pass through rate limiting before the endpoint filter. A single strict login bucket can therefore lock users out while they type. Use separate bounded partitions for validation and real submissions. To tell the two apart, check the endpoint's InertiaPrecognitionMetadata as well as InertiaPrecognition.IsPrecognitive(request) . The header alone does not guarantee that the handler is skipped. Do not use GetNoLimiter for validation, because validators consume CPU and may query a database. When the metadata is present the handler is skipped, so the validation bucket does not allow credential attempts. When the rate limiter rejects a precognitive request, set Precognition: true on the 429 response. The header lets the client recognize the response. The validation request still rejects, so provide a retry or error message. Run UseRouting , UseRateLimiter , UseInertia and UseInertiaAntiforgery in that order. The example below shows a complete policy. The following AddServices method is copied from the Minimal API sample's LoginDemo class. The sample's generation field exists only to reset E2E test buckets. Real apps can partition on a stable client identity that suits their deployment. Import System.Globalization , System.Threading.RateLimiting and Microsoft.AspNetCore.RateLimiting . Declare private static int generation; and private static int submissions; in the LoginDemo class. The complete sample class includes LoginForm , LoginPage , and the reset helper: Call AddServices before you build the app. The sample also adds 429 to error-page handling for real Inertia submissions, because 429 is not a default error-page status: Map an error page with a retry message. Precognitive requests that accept JSON keep their 429 response and Precognition: true header. Attach the policy to the endpoint: The sample routes use this method: The sample partitions by remote IP for demonstration. When your app runs behind a proxy, configure trusted forwarded headers. Choose a partition key that suits your authentication and abuse model. Testing Use an Inertia.Net.Testing client that keeps cookies. Load the form page and attach its XSRF token to each request. This test covers an endpoint that validates email : Import System.Net.Http.Json and Inertia.Net.Testing . Testing shows the client and token setup. Protocol reference Header Direction Meaning --- --- --- Precognition: true Request and response Identifies a validation request and response Precognition-Validate-Only Request Comma-separated client field paths whose errors are returned Precognition-Success: true Response Validation succeeded (204) Vary: Precognition Response Varies the response by request type A validation failure returns 422 . A rate limiter may return 429 . InertiaPrecognition.IsPrecognitive(HttpRequest) checks the header. InertiaPrecognitionMetadata identifies endpoints whose handler is skipped for precognitive requests.

title: AI agents
description: Give coding agents the context and conventions they need to build Inertia.Net pages correctly.
headings: Point the agent at the docs
Let the agent check its own work
body: An Inertia.Net app is a good fit for coding agents: - The backend and the frontend live in one project. - A feature follows one request path: endpoint, props, page component. - There is no API contract or client router for the agent to keep in sync. The main thing an agent needs is to know the conventions. This page gives you that context in a form you can paste into your project. Choose the right reference - Building an app? Start with First 10 minutes, then read the guide for the feature you need. - Changing the adapter? Read the repository's AGENTS.md , docs/protocol.md , and the README's For AI agents section. They explain the source files, tests and protocol rules. Do not apply repository-maintenance rules to an unrelated consuming app. - Looking for a complete Inertia example? Use Kitchen Sink, the official v3 demo. You need to translate its Laravel handlers to C . The client-side Inertia patterns are the reference. Keep examples honest: - Name the file being changed. - Say whether a snippet is a complete file or a fragment. - Run the checks you report. Do not guess API names from another server adapter. Point the agent at the docs The documentation is published as plain text for language models: URL Contents --- --- /llms.txt An index of every page with a one-line summary, following the llms.txt format. /llms-full.txt The whole documentation in one Markdown file. Agents that can fetch URLs can read these files directly. For agents that cannot, download llms-full.txt into your repository, for example as docs/inertia-net.md . Then reference the file from your agent instructions. Add an AGENTS.md section Most coding agents read a project instruction file: - AGENTS.md for Codex and many others - CLAUDE.md for Claude Code - .github/copilot-instructions.md for GitHub Copilot - .cursor/rules for Cursor Copy this section into your instruction file. Adjust the paths and framework to match your app. If you use Vue or Svelte, change the component path and extension. Asking for a feature Agents do better with a request that names both ends of the feature. For example: Add a /projects page. The endpoint returns Projects/Index with a paginated projects prop using Merge and the InfiniteScroll component, and a deferred stats prop. Add a create form that posts to /projects , validates CreateProjectInput with .WithInertiaValidation() , and redirects back with a toast flash message. Add a test with Inertia.Net.Testing for the page component and props. A request like this tells the agent which props to use, how validation is wired, and how to check the result with testing helpers. Let the agent check its own work Agents are most reliable when they can verify a change. Inertia.Net gives them a few cheap checks: - Compile-time types. With generated TypeScript types, a prop renamed in C breaks the client build. The client build script ( npm run build , bun run build , pnpm run build or yarn run build ) therefore catches mismatches. - Response tests. Inertia.Net.Testing asserts the component name and props without a browser. Ask the agent to add one test per page. - Missing components. In Development, DevTools checks report a Render call whose page component does not exist. dotnet new inertia -n MyApp --framework react creates an app with pages, a validated form, flash messages, CSRF and Vite already set up. Starting an agent from the template gives the agent working examples of every convention above.

title: DevTools
description: Record visits for the Inertia DevTools extension and catch missing page components during development.
body: Inertia DevTools lets you see what your browser sent and what ASP.NET Core returned for an Inertia visit. Try it in the starter DevTools lets you inspect a visit without changing its response. Its read API, the endpoints that return the recorded entries, leaves pending errors and flash messages alone. Apps hosted under a path such as /admin report that path to the extension. Request URLs are absolute. Sensitive query values are redacted in the recorded copy, not in your real request. Entries live in memory and disappear on restart. Source-call locations are not collected, so some “open in editor” links are unavailable. Keep the read API private, because recorded entries can include user data. 1. Install the browser extension using the Inertia.js DevTools guide. 2. Start the app and Vite from First 10 minutes. Open http://localhost:5180/todos , open your browser's developer tools, and select the Inertia panel. 3. Submit an empty todo title. Select the visit in the timeline and look at the request and the resulting page data. The validation message is under props.errors.title . The starter enables recording in Development. To add recording to an existing app, use the setup below. Enable DevTools The list endpoint returns metadata summaries. Fetch /entries/{id} for props, HTTP bodies and route details. Ordinary textual and JSON responses are captured up to MaxResponseBytes . Binary, explicitly streamed and oversized responses are omitted. Parsed multipart forms include file names, sizes and MIME types, never file contents. Unparsed uploads are not read only for recording. Render source locations are included when debug symbols are available. Published or Native AOT applications may not retain them. Malformed structured bodies and invalid UTF-8 are omitted, because a raw-text fallback could expose an unredacted secret. To exclude paths, use o.ExcludePaths.Add("/health") or o.ExcludePaths.Add("/assets/ ") in AddInertiaDevTools(o = ...) . Untagged requests use the global entry/byte/age limits. MaxEntriesPerTab applies only when a browser tab ID is supplied. Each request through UseInertia() gets an X-Inertia-Devtools-Id and an entry in memory. Entries are kept per browser tab, at most MaxEntriesPerTab and MaxEntries , for MaxAge . An entry holds: - request type - timings - headers - bodies - the page object and its props metadata The first page carries the discovery tag that the extension reads. In props, bodies and headers, DevTools replaces a value with [REDACTED] when its name contains password , secret , token , authorization , cookie or api key . Add names with RedactedKeys . Nothing leaves the app. Sensitive query parameters are also redacted in recorded request/page URLs, redirects and URL headers. Actual application URLs are unchanged. Malformed JSON bodies are omitted. Only eligible Inertia text bodies with a known length up to MaxBodyBytes are buffered. Unknown-length nonseekable bodies are omitted as streamed, so recording does not spool bulk requests to disk. A page larger than MaxResponseBytes is recorded without its body and is never copied. The default for MaxResponseBytes is 1 MiB. The entry is marked too-large , with the page size in meta.responseBytes . The browser still receives the whole page. Kept entries are also bounded by MaxTotalBytes . The default for MaxTotalBytes is 64 MiB, and the oldest entries are dropped first. Outside Development, nothing is recorded unless Enabled = true . Outside Development, the read API answers only requests that Authorize accepts. Other requests get 404 . With Pages.Directory set, entries link the component to its file. Page component check To turn on the check, set Pages.Directory : In Development, Render throws when the component has no page file. The message names the closest one: Names match exactly, as the client resolver does, even on case-insensitive file systems. Outside Development there is no check and no file access. Pages.Extensions lists the file types. The default is .tsx , .jsx , .ts , .js , .vue and .svelte . Generated TypeScript The development startup also writes TypeScript declarations when o.TypeScript.OutputPath is set. The startup writes the file only when the content changed. See TypeScript types. What to check before deploying - Pages.Directory can stay configured. It is inactive outside Development. - DevTools recording is off unless explicitly enabled. - The generated TypeScript file is committed if the client build type-checks in CI. - Production logs do not contain the DevTools read API. Without an Authorize callback, the read API responds only in Development. Requests must come from this machine through a loopback connection to a loopback host name such as localhost . They must have no X-Forwarded-For , Forwarded , X-Forwarded-Host , X-Real-IP or Via header. Set Authorize to allow access from a container or another machine. A reverse proxy on the same machine makes remote requests look local if it adds none of those headers. Set Authorize in that case too. If recording is enabled outside Development without an Authorize callback, the app logs a warning and the read API returns 404. Map the read API with MapInertiaDevTools() and authorize its users. The recorder's process-wide latch stays active after first use. The process-wide latch for parallel-prop planning does too.

title: First 10 minutes
description: Run your first app, change a C# validation rule, and see the result in your browser.
headings: 3. Follow the form from the browser to C
body: You'll run a small todo app, submit a form, and change how C validates it. The starter sets up ASP.NET Core, your frontend, and Vite for you. To see a complete app first, explore Kitchen Sink, the official Inertia.js v3 sample app. It uses Laravel and Vue. This guide runs the same server-driven page model on .NET. 1. Create the app Install the .NET 10 SDK. The commands below also need Node.js 22.12 or newer with npm. To check what you have, run dotnet --list-sdks and look for a 10.0 SDK, then run node --version to see the Node version. Run these commands in the folder where you want to create MyApp . For Vue or Svelte, use --framework vue or --framework svelte in the dotnet new inertia command. For .NET 11, install the .NET 11 SDK and add --tfm net11.0 . Leave Vite running. In a second terminal, open the same MyApp folder and start the server. Open http://localhost:5180/todos in your browser. That is the address dotnet watch prints. Vite also prints an address on port 5173. Vite uses that address to serve JavaScript, CSS and live updates to the page. 2. Change a C validation rule 1. With the title empty, click Add . The page shows an error below the input. 2. In Program.cs , find NewTodo and change StringLength(100) to StringLength(10) . Save the file, then restart the server to load the new rule. To restart, press Ctrl+C in the server terminal and run dotnet watch again. Leave Vite running. 3. Enter Buy groceries and click Add . The new error shows the 10-character limit. Then try Buy milk . The todo appears in the list. 3. Follow the form from the browser to C In Program.cs , MapPost tells ASP.NET Core what to run when the browser submits to /todos . The name todos.store also gives the frontend a typed function for this route. WithInertiaValidation() checks the rules on NewTodo.Title . If validation fails, Inertia.Net sends the browser back to the page with the error. If the title passes, the handler adds the todo and sends back a one-time success message. Open the page file for your frontend: ClientApp/pages/Todos/Index.tsx , Index.vue , or Index.svelte . The excerpts below show how the form uses the generated route and displays form.errors.title . 4. Try the development tools Follow the route in your editor. Jump to the definition of routes.todos.store() . The starter generates ClientApp/types/routes.ts from your named C endpoints. That function supplies both the URL and the HTTP method to the form. Explore the data your page receives. Find InertiaPages['Todos/Index'] in the page component. To see the type, hover over todos in your editor or open ClientApp/types/inertia.d.ts . The starter generates that declaration from the C TodosPage record in Program.cs . Inspect a submission in your browser. The starter already records visits in Development. Open the Inertia panel and submit an empty title again. Then inspect the request and the page data that contains the error. Install the browser extension and open the panel Next steps - Test a form submission to check the validation error in a .NET test. - Add Inertia to an existing ASP.NET Core app to bring the same workflow to your own project.

title: Vite
description: Manifest tags, the dev-server hot file, asset base URLs, prefetching and CSP nonces.
body: ViteAssets renders the tags for the @vite(...) token and the tag helper. It is a singleton, and you can also use it directly as vite.RenderTags(httpContext, "resources/js/app.tsx") . Production In production, Inertia.Net reads wwwroot/build/.vite/manifest.json . For older Vite, it falls back to wwwroot/build/manifest.json . It parses the manifest once and pre-renders the tags to UTF-8. For each entry it emits, in order: 1. for the entry's CSS and the CSS of its static imports, recursively and deduplicated; 2. for the entry file; 3. for each static import. URLs are {PathBase}/{BuildDirectory}/{file} so apps under a path base work, or {AssetBaseUrl}/{file} . If an entry is missing from the manifest, Inertia.Net throws an exception that lists the available entries. If the manifest is missing, the exception lists the paths Inertia.Net looked in. Preload the current page For a Vite app that lazy-loads its pages, map the final Inertia component name to the manifest key for that page: Use the actual manifest paths and the correct extension for your frontend, such as .vue or .svelte . Return null for pages you want to skip. The HTML root template and Razor root view emit a module preload for the current page when its separate JavaScript chunk is reachable from the entry. The hint uses the same asset URL and nonce as other Vite tags. The dev server, eager bundles, and JSON visits need no hint. After-load prefetch continues to handle other page chunks. Development While the dev server runs, the tags are @vite/client and the entry from the dev server origin, plus the React Refresh preamble for @viteReactRefresh . The dev server counts as running when: - o.Vite.DevServerUrl is set (always, in any environment), or - the environment is Development and the hot file ( wwwroot/hot by default) exists and contains the origin. Your Vite config writes the hot file. The @inertiajs/vite plugin does not write one, so the samples include a small plugin that does. Built assets are served from /build/ , so the Vite base is /build/ for a build. The dev server must serve from the root because Inertia.Net emits {origin}/@vite/client and {origin}/{entry} . Use base: command === 'build' ? '/build/' : '/' . Options Inertia.Net accepts only plain http(s) origins without quotes or markup from the hot file or DevServerUrl , because the origin is echoed into a script. When AssetBaseUrl is set, Vite's own base must match it, so that lazily imported chunks resolve against the CDN too. In your Vite config: Prefetching Page components resolved with lazy import.meta.glob are separate chunks that the browser downloads only when a page needs them. o.Vite.Prefetch downloads them after the page loads, at low priority, so the next navigation does not wait: The tags get one small inline script. The script lists the chunks the entries can import later: dynamic imports, then their static imports and CSS. Chunks that are already loaded are left out. The script is rendered once per entry set. Content Security Policy With a nonce-based CSP, set o.CspNonce to the request's nonce. Every script and stylesheet tag Inertia.Net writes then carries the nonce: - the page - the Vite tags - the React refresh preamble - the prefetch script, whose links get the nonce too The nonce must be base64 or base64url. Anything else throws. Cached tags are split where the nonce goes, so a nonce costs one copy of the tag bytes per request and no re-rendering. Use app.UseStaticFiles() with a long Cache-Control for /build/assets , or app.MapStaticAssets() when the client is built before dotnet publish . See Deploying.

title: Props
description: Lazy, optional, deferred, merged, once, cached and rescued page data.
body: Props are the data a page receives. Render(component, props) takes an InertiaProps , a string-keyed dictionary, or a typed object. Inertia.Net walks nested InertiaProps and dictionaries, so you can nest props at any depth. Every page has an errors prop. The keys of a page's props come in this order: errors , shared props, then page props. Choose how to load data Start with a plain value. Use a lazy loader when the query should run only if the response needs that prop. Use Defer when the page should open before a slow query finishes. Use Optional when the data is needed only on request. Once keeps a value on the client across visits. Cache keeps a value on the server. They solve different problems. Large integer IDs JavaScript cannot represent every 64-bit integer exactly. Set o.PreserveBigIntegers = true at registration to wrap unsafe integers as $bigint markers. The v3 client reads the markers as BigInt . The default is false. To override that choice for one page, return Render("Orders/Show", props).PreserveBigIntegers() or .PreserveBigIntegers(false) . Props and flash use the same setting. This is a handler fragment. C 15 unions (.NET 11). A prop can have a union type, for example public union Subject(User, Team); . Inertia.Net writes such a prop as the JSON of its active case, with no wrapper or discriminator, through your source-generated JsonSerializerContext . Partial reloads select it like any other prop. Inertia.Net does not resolve an InertiaProp ( Defer , Optional , ...) stored inside a union case, so keep lazy props at the page level. The prop factories C\ Behavior --- --- ["title"] = "Hi" A plain value. Sent on every response that includes the key. Prop(() = ...) Lazy: the loader runs only when the prop is part of the response. Always(value) or Always(() = ...) Sent even when a partial reload does not ask for it. Optional(() = ...) Never sent on the first visit, only when a partial reload asks for it. Defer(() = ..., group: "name") Left out of the first response. The client loads it right away with its group. Merge(value) The client appends the new value to its current one. DeepMerge(value) The client deep merges the value. Once(() = ...) Resolved once and remembered by the client. Scroll(page, wrapper: "data", metadata) An infinite-scroll prop with paging metadata. Every lazy factory ( Prop , Always , Optional , Defer , Merge , DeepMerge , Once , Scroll ) accepts five loader shapes: The cancellation token a loader receives is HttpContext.RequestAborted . An async lambda always binds to the awaiting overload, never to “a prop whose value is a Task”. Fluent methods mutate and return the same instance: .Once(key?, until?) , .As(key) , .Until(ttl) , .Fresh() , .Append(path?, matchOn?) , .Prepend(path?, matchOn?) , .DeepMerge() , .MatchOn(params keys) , .Defer(group) , .WithGroup(group) , .Rescue() , .Parallel() , .Cache(key, duration) and .Cache(key, duration, staleFor?, tags?) . Fresh() makes a prop a once prop, and WithGroup() makes it deferred. Repeated MatchOn() calls add keys. Root Append() and Prepend() are mutually exclusive, and combining them throws. Fluent methods mutate the prop, so create prop instances per request. Do not share prop instances across requests. Resolution order By default, loaders run one after another, in prop order. A loader runs only when its prop is included in the response. Because loaders run one at a time, a scoped EF Core DbContext is safe to use in several loaders. Inertia.Net buffers the page before sending it, so a loader that throws never produces a half-written 200 . Parallel props Mark independent async loaders with .Parallel() to start them together: - Only Task and ValueTask loaders can be parallel. Parallel() throws for values and synchronous loaders. - At most InertiaOptions.Props.MaxConcurrency loaders run at once per render. The default is 4. - Top-level props and props inside literal objects ( InertiaProps and other string-keyed dictionaries) start early. Parallel props anywhere else resolve in turn. - Loaders of props that are not part of the response never start. - If a loader fails, Inertia.Net cancels and awaits the others. The render then fails with the first failure in prop order. A Rescue() d prop fails alone. A parallel loader must not use the request's DbContext or other non-thread-safe scoped services, and must not touch HttpContext . Give each loader its own context through IDbContextFactory or its own scope. Scoped services in loaders Prop (...) hands a loader a service from the request, without capturing it in a closure: - A loader that runs during the request gets the request's instance. This is the same DbContext the handler used. - A .Parallel() loader gets a scope of its own, so two parallel loaders never share a DbContext . The scope is disposed when the loader finishes. - A stale-while-revalidate refresh runs after the response, in a new scope. That scope is disposed when the refresh ends. - If the service is not registered, the render fails with the prop's path and the service type. Deferred props Defer leaves the prop out of the first response and lists it under deferredProps . The client asks for each group as soon as the page is mounted. See Deferred props for the client component and the request rules. Merge props The full behavior is in Merging props. Once props When the client already holds the key, it sends X-Inertia-Except-Once-Props . The value is then left out, and the onceProps entry stays. See Once props. Cached props .Cache(key, duration) keeps a prop's value as JSON in the cache. The default cache is the app's IMemoryCache . A cache hit costs neither the query nor serialization. Every request that uses a key gets the same value. Put the user, tenant or anything else the value depends on in the key. Keys live in their own cache space and cannot collide with the app's own entries. Caching only changes how a prop loads. Optional, deferred, merged, once and scroll props keep their behavior, and their metadata is written from the cache too. A parallel cached prop does not start its loader on a cache hit. A rescued failure is not cached. Removing and replacing values. Inject IInertiaCache where the data changes: ClearPropsAsync() removes every cached prop. ClearSsrAsync() removes every cached render. SetPropAsync serializes the value the way a prop of that type is serialized, and takes the same staleFor and tags . The default store keeps cached props in the app's IMemoryCache , with no size limit of their own. Set o.Props.CacheMaxBytes to cap them. Cached props then go in a private cache, and the least recently used ones are evicted past the cap. Stale-while-revalidate. staleFor keeps serving a value after its duration. The first request that reads a stale value gets the stale value at once, and the loader runs after the response has been sent. After duration + staleFor , the loader runs during the request again. - When the response completes, Inertia.Net queues the refreshes on a bounded background worker. The response does not wait for the loader. Loaders that use staleFor must use singleton dependencies, or create an independent scope inside the loader with IServiceScopeFactory.CreateAsyncScope() or IDbContextFactory . Do not capture request-scoped services or HttpContext . - The worker accepts 64 pending refreshes and runs up to 4 at a time. It cancels each refresh after 30 seconds, and cancels all of them on host shutdown. When the queue is full, Inertia.Net drops the refresh and logs a warning. The stale value keeps its existing expiration. Monitor inertia.cache.refresh.dropped , tagged with inertia.cache.kind=prop ssr . - One refresh runs per key and app instance at a time. A refresh that finds the value fresh again skips its loader. - An IInertiaCache removal ( RemovePropAsync , RemoveByTagAsync , ClearPropsAsync ) can happen while a fill or refresh is running. If the loader started before the removal of its key or of one of its tags, on the same app instance, the fill or refresh does not store its value. The request still gets the value. Removing another key or tag does not affect the fill or refresh. - A refresh that fails is logged as a warning, and the stale value stays. The next stale read tries again. Another store. Props and SSR renders live in an IInertiaCacheStore . Register your own singleton before or after AddInertia() : The store gets and sets byte arrays by InertiaCacheKey , removes by key and by tag, and reads unknown formats as a miss. While a page renders, a store that throws is logged, at most once every 30 seconds, and counts as a miss. IInertiaCache lets the exception through. For a store shared by every app instance, Inertia.Net.Redis registers one with AddInertiaRedisCache(...) . See Redis cache. Typed page props A typed object is AOT-friendly. Inertia.Net walks the object through its JsonTypeInfo . It resolves members of type InertiaProp , and the rest is serialized normally. Under Native AOT, register UsersPage and its value types in your JsonSerializerContext . Anonymous types work only when reflection-based serialization is enabled, so they do not work under AOT. Dot keys A top-level key containing dots is unpacked. ["user.name"] = "Ann" becomes "user": { "name": "Ann" } . Cached props under dot keys use the cache too. BigInteger safety With o.PreserveBigIntegers = true , integers beyond ±(2^53 − 1) are written as {"$bigint":"9007199254740993"} and the page gets "preserveBigIntegers": true . Rescue .Rescue() keeps a page alive when one prop fails: If the loader throws, Inertia.Net logs the exception and leaves the prop out of props . The prop's path goes to "rescuedProps": ["recommendations"] . Without .Rescue() , the exception propagates normally. Cancellation of the request is never rescued.

title: Multiple apps and libraries
description: Mount a second Inertia UI under its own path, with its own shared props, asset version, state cookie, root view, error pages and SSR.
headings: What a mount keeps to itself
A root view shipped by a library
body: One ASP.NET Core app can serve more than one Inertia UI. A typical case is a library, such as an admin dashboard, that ships its own prebuilt client. A host app that already uses Inertia.Net mounts the library under /dashboard . Each UI is a mount : a named InertiaOptions that app.UseInertia(name) selects inside an app.Map(...) branch. The default mount is the one AddInertia(...) and UseInertia() configure, so existing apps do not change. What a mount keeps to itself Per mount Shared by all mounts --- --- Shared props ( o.Share ) and every other InertiaOptions setting IInertiaCache and the cache store (choose distinct InertiaProp.Cache(key) keys) Asset version: the 409 check only compares against the mount's own version IInertiaLive and the SignalR hub State cookie: .Inertia.State.{name} and .Inertia.Previous.{name} by default Metrics (named mounts add an inertia.mount tag) and DevTools Root view: the mount's RootView file, or a keyed IInertiaRootView Antiforgery and data protection Vite manifest, SSR servers, managed Node processes, TypeScript output The SSR HttpClient (its ConnectTimeout comes from the default mount) Error pages registered with AddInertiaErrorPages(name, ...) Register and map a mount Map sets the request's path base, so these stay inside /dashboard : - page URLs - Back() fallbacks - Vite asset URLs - the previous-URL cookie Calling AddInertia("dashboard", ...) again adds to that mount's configuration. Startup fails when UseInertia(name) names a mount that was never registered, or when two mounts share a state or previous-URL cookie name. A root view shipped by a library A library cannot rely on a file in the host's content root. Instead, register a keyed IInertiaRootView that writes an embedded template: Error pages per mount A mount renders only the error components registered for it, because another mount's components are not in its bundle. A mount without AddInertiaErrorPages(name, ...) leaves its errors to the rest of the pipeline. SSR, health checks and TypeScript Each mount has its own SSR gateway. When o.Ssr.UseNodeProcess() is set, each mount also has its own managed Node processes. Give each mount its own BasePort . Check a mount's SSR servers with a health check: o.TypeScript.OutputPath is per mount too, so each client gets its own generated declarations. For library authors Expose one registration call and one mapping call, and keep the mount name private to the library: Mounts are adapter configuration. The Inertia protocol on the wire does not change.

title: Live props
description: Props that refresh themselves when the server broadcasts an event.
body: A live prop refreshes itself when the server broadcasts an event. The page response says which props listen to which events. The client subscribes to the channels of those events. When an event arrives, the client reloads the affected props or applies the values the event carries. Your components never subscribe or clean up. Three pieces make it work: 1. An event , defined once as a LiveEvent and shared by both sides. 2. A prop marked .Live(event) , which puts its listeners in the page's liveProps . 3. A publish through IInertiaLive , delivered to subscribers by a transport. Live props need @inertiajs/react , @inertiajs/vue3 or @inertiajs/svelte 3.11.0 or later. Older clients ignore liveProps . Define each event once A LiveEvent is an event name on a LiveChannel . You use the same LiveEvent value to declare the prop and to publish the event, so the two sides always match. A channel is LiveChannel.Public , Private , Presence or EncryptedPrivate . Channel names carry no prefix. A transport adds private- or presence- itself when its protocol needs one. Mark props live The page lists every listener, including the listeners of props it left out: Call Effect --- --- .Live(event) Adds a listener. Repeatable: call it once per event. .Live(channel, "Created", "Deleted") Listens to several events on one channel. Live(() = ..., event) The factory form of Prop(...).Live(event) . .Throttle(window) The shortest time between two reloads of the prop. The client's default is one second. What combines with live Prop Live? Notes --- --- --- Prop , Always , shared props Yes Defer , Optional Yes Listeners are reported even while the value is left out. Once Yes A once prop the client already holds stays subscribed. Rescue , Parallel Yes A rescued prop stays subscribed. The next event fetches it again. Cache Yes Publishing does not evict the cache. Remove the entry with IInertiaCache first. Merge , DeepMerge , Scroll No A live prop is replaced whole, so these throw InvalidOperationException . Reload them from the page instead: see Reloading scroll and merge props. A live prop inside an array reloads its whole array, as every partial reload of an array descendant does. Prefer keyed objects for lists that change often. Shared live props A shared live prop keeps something current on every page, such as a notification bell: Publish events AddInertiaLive() registers IInertiaLive , the service you publish events through. A transport registers the IInertiaLiveBroadcaster that delivers what IInertiaLive publishes. - Without values , every client reloads the live props that listen to the event, each with its own request and its own data. - With values , the props named in the values are updated in place. The values are keyed by prop path ( "auth.user" stays a flat key). Values use the page serializer options, so they match what a reload returns. Under Native AOT, the type needs to be in your registered JSON context, like any prop type. - exceptSocketId leaves one connection out, usually the client that made the change. The client sends its id as X-Socket-Id , and HttpContext.InertiaRequest().SocketId reads it. The client supplies the header, so it is only ever used to exclude a connection. A broadcast reaches every client on the channel. Only publish values that everyone allowed on the channel may see. When a value depends on the user, publish without values and let each client reload its own data. A broadcaster delivers this payload: Resolve values for a broadcast Use plain values with IInertiaLive.PublishAsync when you already have the data. If you have prop definitions instead, resolve them first. This handler fragment assumes http , orders , id , live , orderUpdated and ct are in scope: Visit filters do not restrict a broadcast. Optional, deferred and once values all resolve. A rescued value is left out. Dot-path keys stay flat. No page or DevTools entry is created. Only publish values that every subscriber of the channel is allowed to see. On the client Read a live prop like any other prop. useProp exposes the prop's loading state. The live router event is cancelable, so a listener can hold an update back, for example to show a "new posts" button instead: SignalR Inertia.Net.Live.SignalR runs the transport inside your app. It provides: - a SignalR hub the browser subscribes to - channel authorization - the broadcaster that IInertiaLive publishes through Apps created with dotnet new inertia ship the client transport as ClientApp/lib/inertia-signalr.ts . In other apps, copy the file into your app. Then turn the transport on: @microsoft/signalr loads on the first subscription, so pages without live props never download it. When a dropped connection comes back, the transport joins its channels again. Inertia then reloads every live prop once, which catches up on missed events. Who may join a channel Channel Who joins --- --- Public Anyone who reaches the hub. Set o.AuthorizePublicChannels = true to ask the authorizer too. Private , Presence , EncryptedPrivate Only connections the authorizer allows. With no authorizer, nobody joins. For rules that need services, implement ILiveChannelAuthorizer and register it with o.Authorize () . The authorizer is created for each subscription, with constructor injection. SignalR has no presence member lists or end-to-end encryption, so presence and encrypted-private channels are authorized like private ones. The hub answers requests from other origins with 403. Add trusted origins to o.AllowedOrigins . The origin check takes the place of antiforgery tokens on the hub. Connections close when their authentication expires. SignalR groups exist on one server only. When you run several instances, add a Redis backplane ( AddSignalR().AddStackExchangeRedis(...) ) or Azure SignalR Service. Without one of these, a publish reaches only the clients connected to the instance that sent it. The package README lists the client options, how channels map to SignalR groups, and the security notes. Reloading scroll and merge props A Scroll(...) or Merge(...) prop cannot be live, because a live reload would merge the reloaded page into the list. Reload such a prop from the page instead, with ClientApp/lib/inertia-live-reload.ts , which dotnet new inertia apps include: liveReload works like this: - Events within debounce milliseconds become one reload. The default is 250. - A reload waits for a visit that is in progress. - The scroll position is kept. - The client that caused the event ( exceptSocketId ) is not reloaded. reset replaces the prop instead of merging it, so the reload brings no duplicates. The SignalR client transport delivers a channel's events to every subscriber. See Typed routes for routes.ts . Custom transports The page metadata and the payload do not depend on SignalR, so any transport works: - Pusher-protocol servers (Reverb, Soketi, Ably, Pusher) work with the client's built-in pusher() or echo() transport. On the server, implement IInertiaLiveBroadcaster with your server's publish API. - Anything else (Action Cable, server-sent events, Azure Web PubSub): implement IInertiaLiveBroadcaster on the server and a LiveTransport on the client. A broadcaster has one method. It receives the channel, the finished payload and the connection to skip: Testing InertiaPage.LiveProps holds the live metadata, and HasLive asserts it. Write the channel as "{type}:{name}" : Limits, proxies and authorization changes SignalR defaults to 64 subscriptions per connection and a 200-character channel name. Configure MaxSubscriptionsPerConnection and MaxChannelNameLength through the SignalR options. Both must be positive. Behind a TLS-terminating proxy, configure trusted forwarded headers once and run UseForwardedHeaders() before the hub. The origin and scheme checks then see the external address. Authorization is checked when a client subscribes, not continuously. If access changes, disconnect the client, or use a transport or application strategy that enforces revocation. A removed event can tell the UI to update, but it is not a security mechanism for revoking access.

title: Learn from Kitchen Sink
description: Explore the official Inertia.js v3 demo, then use the same ideas in ASP.NET Core.
headings: Translate the server, keep the idea
Check the whole request, not just the JSON
body: The official Inertia.js v3 sample application is Kitchen Sink . It combines a small CRM with pages that show forms, navigation, deferred data, prefetching, state, layouts and error handling. - Open the live demo - Read the source - Read Inertia's demo guide Kitchen Sink uses Laravel and Vue , not Inertia.Net. Its client-side patterns still apply: the server chooses a page, passes props, validates forms and redirects after submissions. Replace the Laravel handler with a C endpoint. The public demo resets its database every midnight. Use it respectfully and do not enter private information. Pick one flow to learn Try this in Kitchen Sink Then read this .NET guide --- --- Open a page and follow a link Pages and responses Submit an invalid form Validation and errors Show a message after saving Flash data Load a slow section after the page opens Deferred props Refresh only one list Partial reloads Append another page of results Infinite scroll Show a friendly error page Error pages Translate the server, keep the idea These are handler fragments, not complete application files: For a runnable .NET example, use this repository's sample apps, or create a starter with First 10 minutes. The samples use Minimal APIs with React, MVC with Vue, and FastEndpoints with Svelte. Kitchen Sink is the upstream learning reference. These samples show the .NET setup. Check the whole request, not just the JSON When you add a feature, check that: - the first visit works - a link updates the page without reloading the document - an invalid form shows errors - a partial reload sends only the selected props plus always props - an asset-version change triggers a full reload These checks catch problems that a JSON snapshot alone can miss.

title: Merging props
description: Append, prepend, deep merge and match items instead of replacing the client's value.
body: By default, a reloaded prop replaces the client's value. A merge prop tells the client to combine the new value with the value it already has. Pagination, chat messages and incremental lists work this way. C\ Metadata Client behavior --- --- --- Merge(v) mergeProps: ["key"] Append to the existing array Prop(...).Prepend() prependProps: ["key"] Prepend Merge(v).Append("path") mergeProps: ["key.path"] Append at a nested path Prop(...).Prepend("path") prependProps: ["key.path"] Prepend at a nested path DeepMerge(v) deepMergeProps: ["key"] Deep merge objects and arrays .MatchOn("id") matchPropsOn: ["key.id"] Replace items with the same id instead of duplicating them .Append("path", matchOn: "id") matchPropsOn: ["key.path.id"] The match key is relative to the nested path Nested paths The path before the wrapper stays on the client. Only the value below the path is merged. Resetting a merge The client can ask for a fresh value instead of a merge by listing the path in X-Inertia-Reset : Merge metadata is skipped for paths in the reset list. On partial reloads, it is also skipped for paths the reload did not ask for. Match on a stable key .MatchOn("id") replaces an item with the same key instead of appending a duplicate. Use a stable, unique key from your data. Without a match key, incremental updates append every item again. Deep merge DeepMerge recursively combines objects. Arrays are merged by index. Use MatchOn when you need item identity. On a partial reload, merge metadata is only emitted for paths the reload asked for. Always still applies independently.

title: Redirects and history
description: Redirects, Back, Location, history encryption, clearing and URL fragments.
body: Inertia requests follow redirects with XHR, which is not always what the browser would do. Inertia.Net adjusts redirect responses so the client behaves correctly. Redirect helpers Back() follows a Referer only when the Referer is an http(s) URL with the request's own host and port.
