body: Inertia.Render(...) does not compile The compiler reports 'Inertia' is a namespace . Call Render(...) without a namespace or class prefix. The namespace Inertia.Net shadows the class name outside the Inertia.Net namespace. The global usings come from the package's buildTransitive props and need enable . Without implicit usings, or with InertiaNetImplicitUsings set to false , add using static Inertia.Net.Inertia; . Inside a namespace that starts with Inertia.Net. , the name Inertia binds to the Inertia.Net.Inertia class. Source generators that emit non- global:: names starting with Inertia then break. Do not put your app's code under an Inertia.Net. namespace. Do one of these three things. Run your package manager’s build script ( npm run build , bun run build , pnpm run build or yarn run build ). Or start the dev server so that the hot file exists in Development. Or set o.Vite.ManifestPath / o.Vite.BuildDirectory . Check that Vite writes .vite/manifest.json ( build.manifest: true , Vite 5 and later) to wwwroot/build . Also check that the build output is part of what you deploy. The @vite("...") argument must equal the manifest key, which is the path relative to the Vite root. The error lists the available entries. TypeLoadException for IValidatableInfo on .NET 11 Could not load type 'Microsoft.Extensions.Validation.IValidatableInfo' (or ValidatableTypeInfo ) means a .NET 10 build is running on .NET 11. Upgrade every Inertia.Net package to 1.8.0 or later and target net11.0 . Do not roll a net10.0 app forward to the .NET 11 runtime. See Installation. My 404 shows the Inertia modal in production Register AddInertiaErrorPages() and call UseInertiaErrorPages() before UseInertia() . Create your error components. See Error pages. Form submissions fail with 419 UseInertiaAntiforgery() rejected a request without a valid X-XSRF-TOKEN . Check these points: - The page was loaded through the middleware. The middleware sets the XSRF-TOKEN cookie. - The cookie reaches the browser. A Secure cookie on plain HTTP is dropped. See Deploying. - All instances share the Data Protection key ring. - UseAuthentication() runs before UseInertiaAntiforgery() . A sign-in or sign-out changes the token. After one, reload the page, or return Back() from OnRejected . Exempt webhooks and token-authenticated APIs with .DisableAntiforgery() or ShouldValidate . The Inertia page component was not found This error means that o.Pages.Directory is set and the component passed to Render(...) has no page file in that directory. Names match exactly, as the client's page resolver does, even on case-insensitive file systems. The message suggests the closest page. Fix the name, or check Pages.Extensions when your pages use another extension. The check runs only in Development. A redirect to another site turns into a 409 This is the ConvertExternalRedirects option, which is on by default. An Inertia request cannot follow a redirect to another origin. Instead, the request gets 409 + X-Inertia-Location and the client does a full visit. If this happens for your own host, the app is behind a proxy that does not forward the scheme. See Deploying, or use relative redirects. To disable the conversion, set o.ConvertExternalRedirects = false . The root view resolves outside the content root RootView and WithRootView(...) take a path relative to the content root. Absolute paths and .. are refused. Never derive these paths from request data. The page keeps reloading, or a request loops with 409 A 409 means the asset version differs between the client and the server. A loop means the two versions never match. Usually the version changes on every request: a VersionResolver returns a new value each time, or a file watcher regenerates the manifest. Another usual cause is that different instances behind a load balancer serve different builds. Use a stable version string. In Development the manifest hash changes after each vite build , which is expected once. A blank page at localhost:5173 http://localhost:5173 is the Vite dev server. It serves assets and hot-reload updates to your app. It has no pages of its own, so it shows a blank page. Instead, open the ASP.NET Core URL that dotnet watch or dotnet run prints. In the starter templates that URL is http://localhost:5180 . The dev server tags do not appear Inertia.Net reads the hot file only when ASPNETCORE ENVIRONMENT=Development . Check that wwwroot/hot exists and contains http://localhost:5173 , or set o.Vite.DevServerUrl . Also set base: '/' for the dev server in vite.config . The root template was not found, or @inertia is missing RootView is relative to the content root . Copy app.html to the output and publish directories ( CopyToOutputDirectory , CopyToPublishDirectory ). The template must contain @inertia . Flash data or errors disappear Browsers limit the state cookie to about 4 KB. Flash less data, or use o.State.UseSession() . If the app runs on several instances, share Data Protection keys. If the browser never sends the cookie back, check the cookie's Secure flag when the app runs on HTTP behind a proxy that does not forward X-Forwarded-Proto . Validation errors do not show up (Minimal API) Use .WithInertiaValidation() on the endpoint. Without it, the built-in AddValidation() filter returns a 400 problem details response that the Inertia client cannot use. Make sure the model types are public . Validation keys do not match my field names Keys use dotted indices and available JSON member aliases. Minimal API and MVC use the page serializer’s HTTP JSON options. FastEndpoints uses its binding serializer policy. Keep these aligned with client field names. Metadata-free or custom resolver paths can fall back to naming-policy conversion. See Validation. InertiaProp values can only be serialized by Inertia.Net An InertiaProp is in a place that Inertia.Net does not walk: - a Flash(...) value - a read-only dictionary type that does not implement IDictionary - a type with a custom converter Inertia.Net walks lists, typed dictionaries ( Dictionary with any key type), object members and IDictionary . Put props in InertiaProps , or declare the member as InertiaProp (or object ) on the typed page object. Native AOT: JsonTypeInfo metadata was not provided Add the type to your JsonSerializerContext and chain it with ConfigureHttpJsonOptions . To find these errors early, set JsonSerializerIsReflectionEnabledByDefault=false in regular builds. See Native AOT. SSR does not run and there is no error SSR falls back to client rendering on any failure. Look for the warnings Inertia SSR failed (...) and Inertia SSR skipped (...) . The first includes the server's hint. Check these points: - o.Ssr.Mode and Urls . - The Node server is running ( GET /health ). With UseNodeProcess() , look for Inertia.Net.Ssr log lines. - BundlePath points at the built file. - The path is not in ExcludePaths . - The page is under MaxPageBytes . To see the failure, set Mode = SsrMode.Required in Development. SSR skipped (circuit-open) or (overloaded) - circuit-open : the server failed CircuitBreaker.FailureThreshold times in a row and is skipped for BreakDuration . The earlier Inertia SSR failed warnings say why. - overloaded : more renders arrived than Concurrency.MaxActive plus MaxQueued , or one waited longer than QueueTimeout . Add servers or instances, or raise the limits if the server has spare capacity. Several managed instances never become healthy Every instance must listen on its own port. For that, the SSR entry has to read process.env.INERTIA SSR PORT . A bundle built only by @inertiajs/vite listens on the port that was fixed at build time. The SSR output is not hydrated Use the hydrating client entry shown in Server-side rendering and build both bundles from the same sources. The SSR body is marked data-server-rendered="true" . Does it work behind a path base? Yes. The page url keeps the path base, the Vite URLs include it, and Back() works. Can I use Newtonsoft.Json? No. Props use System.Text.Json with the HTTP JSON options. Can I mix Razor Pages or views with Inertia pages? Yes. Inertia handles only the endpoints that return Render(...) . The middleware leaves other responses alone, apart from Vary: X-Inertia . Forms submit invalid data Minimal API endpoints need .WithInertiaValidation() or .WithInertiaPrecognition() and AddValidation() . Endpoint construction throws when validation resolvers are missing. Routing can construct endpoints lazily. See Validation. 419 in tests 1. Use a cookie-preserving client. 2. Load an Inertia page first. 3. Use request.WithXsrfToken(pageResponse) on the form request. See Testing. Precognition: login locks users out while typing Precognitive POSTs pass through rate limiting. Use separate bounded partitions for validation and for submission, and validate on blur. See Precognition. A throttled validation still rejects, so show a retry message. To render a custom Inertia error page for a real submission rejected with 429, add 429 with AddInertiaErrorPages(o = o.StatusCodes.Add(429)) and put UseInertiaErrorPages() before UseRateLimiter() . Precognitive JSON responses keep their 429 and Precognition: true header. 'Location' is a type but is used like a variable The imported static Location name may collide with a type. Call Inertia.Net.Inertia.Location(url) explicitly, or opt out with false and add your own imports. See Configuration. A cached prop loader runs every request Check that the key and duration are stable and the cache store works. Dot-key props support caching. Include every user or tenant dependency in the cache key. A stale refresh needs its own scope and may be dropped when the background queue is full. See Props.

title: Framework comparison
description: Compare complete application stacks: ASP.NET Core with Inertia.Net, Next.js, TanStack Start, Nuxt and Laravel with Inertia. Understand their setup, strengths and measured performance.
headings: What you gain with each setup
Inertia.Net with its caching turned on
Every framework with its caching turned on
What Inertia.Net caches, and what it doesn't
body: Choosing a stack starts with the language, backend framework and way of building that suit your team. Speed and hosting cost matter too. To make those trade-offs easier to see, we built the same small app with five application stacks and measured their particular setups side by side. This page explains what was built, introduces each framework and what it is good at, and then walks through the results in plain terms. The .NET entry is C and ASP.NET Core, with Inertia.Net connecting the backend to React pages . The Laravel entry is PHP and Laravel with Inertia. Next.js, TanStack Start and Nuxt bring their own application structure and rendering tools. Inertia.Net does not make .NET faster. The language, runtime, web framework, database access, rendering and deployment setup all contribute to these results. Inertia.Net provides the page-and-props connection and optional features such as caching. It is not the source of C 's execution speed or ASP.NET Core's concurrency. These numbers cannot isolate adapter overhead or predict every app's performance. What you gain with each setup Stack How you build it What you gain --- --- --- C / ASP.NET Core + Inertia.Net Keep routing, data access and business logic in .NET. Return React, Vue or Svelte pages and props through Inertia instead of designing a separate page API. ASP.NET Core's backend tools and .NET's runtime characteristics, plus a modern component frontend. Inertia.Net supplies the connection, not a faster runtime. TypeScript / Next.js Build around React's App Router, server/client components and Next.js data and rendering conventions. An integrated React application framework, static and server rendering options, and a broad hosting and tooling ecosystem. TypeScript / TanStack Start Use React routes, loaders and server functions with TanStack's typed APIs. A TypeScript-first workflow with closely connected routing and server calls, and explicit control over data loading. TypeScript / Nuxt Build Vue pages with file-based routing, auto-imports, composables and Nitro server routes. A cohesive Vue setup with less wiring, modules and integrated server-rendering tools. PHP / Laravel + Inertia Use Laravel routes, controllers and backend services; return component pages through Inertia. Laravel's conventions and backend ecosystem, with React, Vue or Svelte pages rather than a separately designed page API. For example, choosing .NET with Inertia.Net means keeping your C services and ASP.NET Core infrastructure while adding a component frontend. Choosing Nuxt means adopting its Vue and TypeScript application model. Neither choice is only a different adapter. Each choice changes where your code lives, which tools you use and how you deploy. The short version - The ASP.NET Core + Inertia.Net setup handled the most traffic in the tests shown , from first page loads to form posts to heavy calculations. Its Native AOT build also used the least memory and started fastest. These are whole-stack results, not gains caused by installing the adapter. - TanStack Start is the leanest JavaScript option. It used as little memory as Inertia.Net's normal build and started the fastest of all the server-rendered apps. - Nuxt's API is very quick , but its server-rendered pages were slower than the other JavaScript frameworks except Next.js. - Next.js and Laravel served the fewest requests in this setup. Both still answered in a few milliseconds at everyday traffic levels. - With caching configured for every stack, the .NET setup was still the fastest in this run , by 2 to 6 times over the next best on cached first visits. The cache implementations do different work, as explained below. - At normal traffic every framework is fast enough. The differences matter when traffic spikes, when you pay per server, or when a page does heavy work. What we built Each framework runs the same todo app on the same Postgres database and Redis cache: - Home page : a short list of features. - Todo list : 25 or 100 todos from a table of 10,000, newest first. - Dashboard : totals for the whole table, cached in Redis for 60 seconds. - New todo form : checks four fields and saves the todo, or shows one error per field. - Heavy page : a CPU-intensive calculation, run once on one core and once split across all cores. Each app runs in two modes. In SSR mode the server sends a fully rendered page on the first visit. In SPA mode the server sends an empty shell and the browser renders it. After the first visit, moving between pages only fetches data, in every framework. Before any measuring, a parity check confirms that every app returns exactly the same todos, totals, calculation results and error messages. If one app did less work, the parity check would show it. The frameworks ASP.NET Core with Inertia.Net Inertia.Net lets you write the server in ASP.NET Core and the pages in React, Vue or Svelte, without building a separate API. Controllers or Minimal API handlers return a page name and its data. Inertia's client does the routing in the browser. How it was built here : a Minimal API with React pages, EF Core for the database, InertiaProp.Cache for the dashboard, .NET validation with WithInertiaValidation() , and antiforgery protection on every form. It ran in two builds: - JIT : the normal .NET build, which optimises itself while it runs. - Native AOT : compiled ahead of time into one small executable. EF Core doesn't support Native AOT yet, so this build reads the database with Npgsql directly. See Native AOT. What comes from .NET and ASP.NET Core : the C runtime, concurrent request handling, backend libraries such as EF Core and Identity, and the option of Native AOT. What Inertia.Net adds : returning component pages and props from those endpoints, with Inertia navigation, forms and optional prop/render caching. You keep a .NET backend and a React, Vue or Svelte frontend without building a separate page API. The adapter still does work on each response. It does not make the underlying runtime faster. Next.js Next.js is the most widely used React framework. Its App Router mixes server and client components, and it has its own caching, routing, image handling and a large ecosystem around it. How it was built here : the App Router with server components, Drizzle for the database, zod for validation, and the dashboard cached with 'use cache: remote' and a Redis cache handler. The form posts to a route handler. Strengths : the biggest React ecosystem and community, React Server Components, static generation and incremental regeneration for content sites, and first-class hosting on Vercel and other platforms. TanStack Start TanStack Start is a newer full-stack React framework built on TanStack Router. It focuses on type-safe routes, type-safe server functions and explicit data loading, and runs on Vite with Nitro as its server. How it was built here : file-based routes with loaders and server functions, Drizzle, zod, and the dashboard cached with Nitro's defineCachedFunction stored in Redis. Strengths : end-to-end type safety from route parameters to server calls, a light runtime, very fast startup, and Vite's fast developer experience. It is still young, and its Node server uses Nitro 3, which is a release candidate. Nuxt Nuxt is the main full-stack framework for Vue. It brings file-based pages, auto-imports, data fetching with useFetch , and a server layer for APIs, all on Nitro. How it was built here : Vue pages that fetch their data with useFetch , API routes on Nitro, Drizzle, zod, and the same Nitro cache in Redis as TanStack Start. Nuxt renders Vue, while the other apps render the same React pages. So part of any difference in page rendering comes from Vue, not from Nuxt itself. Strengths : the most complete Vue experience, conventions that remove a lot of setup, a big module ecosystem, and a fast API layer that can be deployed almost anywhere. Laravel Laravel is PHP's most popular framework. With Inertia, its controllers return React, Vue or Svelte pages the same way Inertia.Net does. In this comparison it runs on Octane with FrankenPHP, which keeps the app in memory between requests instead of starting fresh each time. How it was built here : Eloquent models, a Form Request for validation, Cache::remember for the dashboard, and CSRF protection with cookie sessions. Strengths : a developer experience known for being productive, everything built in (auth, queues, mail, scheduling, storage), a huge ecosystem, and the official Inertia adapter, the one Inertia started with. The results To keep labels short, charts and tables call the .NET setup Inertia.Net and the PHP setup Laravel . Read these as ASP.NET Core + Inertia.Net and Laravel + Inertia , with the database, frontend and hosting choices described above. They are not measurements of either adapter alone. The JIT and AOT entries also use different database access libraries, so the difference between them does not come only from the compilation mode. All six apps ran on GitHub's cloud machines. Each test route got its own machine with every app on it, so the apps in any one row of the tables below shared the same hardware. Each app was limited to 2 CPU cores and 2 GB of memory. Every request succeeded, and every server-rendered page really was rendered on the server. Memory, startup and image size Less memory means more apps per server and a smaller hosting bill. Faster startup helps when scaling up under load or running on platforms that start apps on demand. App Memory when idle, SPA / SSR Startup time, SPA / SSR Docker image, SPA / SSR --- ---: ---: ---: Inertia.Net, Native AOT 17 / 46 MB 216 / 514 ms 34 / 98 MB Inertia.Net, JIT 27 / 60 MB 522 / 1,108 ms 125 / 189 MB TanStack Start 28 / 29 MB 263 / 258 ms 166 MB Next.js 72 / 76 MB 715 / 775 ms 185 MB Nuxt 138 / 139 MB 340 / 739 ms 169 MB Laravel 98 / 154 MB 785 / 951 ms 252 / 311 MB In SSR mode the Inertia apps also run a small Node.js process to render pages, which is why their SSR memory is higher. For Laravel the figure includes all its PHP workers. First visits A first visit is what a visitor gets when they open a link or reload the page. In SSR mode the server renders the whole page. This is the todo list with 25 rows: App Pages per second Typical response under full load Typical response at 50 visits per second --- ---: ---: ---: Inertia.Net, Native AOT 3,905 3.9 ms 1.1 ms Inertia.Net, JIT 1,764 6.6 ms 1.2 ms TanStack Start 1,294 11.6 ms 1.4 ms Nuxt 745 19.8 ms 1.9 ms Next.js 364 41.9 ms 4.1 ms Laravel 337 32.4 ms 5.8 ms The last column shows what to expect in practice: at everyday traffic, every framework answers in a few milliseconds. The first column is how much traffic one small server can take before it is saturated. Moving between pages After the first visit, clicking a link only fetches the next page's data as JSON. This is what most interactions in an app cost. App Todo list, per second Dashboard (cached), per second --- ---: ---: Inertia.Net, Native AOT 9,789 12,842 Inertia.Net, JIT 6,155 13,465 Nuxt 5,498 10,262 TanStack Start 3,962 7,153 Next.js 1,512 2,283 Laravel 550 1,056 Nuxt does well here: its API routes are fast, and on the smallest page it matched Inertia.Net. Saving a form The form test posts a new todo. A valid post is checked and saved to the database. An invalid post fails all four checks and returns the error messages. App Valid posts per second Invalid posts per second --- ---: ---: Inertia.Net, Native AOT 2,956 18,299 Inertia.Net, JIT 2,810 16,314 TanStack Start 2,464 12,559 Nuxt 1,996 11,417 Next.js 957 1,841 Laravel 517 854 Saving is limited by the database for every framework, so the fast apps end up close together on valid posts. Invalid posts never touch the database, so they show what the framework itself costs. The Inertia apps also check a forgery-protection token on every post. The JavaScript apps' API routes don't by default. Heavy work The heavy page runs a CPU-intensive calculation. This is mostly a test of the programming language. App Requests per second With 1 / 2 / 4 CPU cores --- ---: ---: Inertia.Net, JIT 1,212 648 / 1,260 / 1,938 Inertia.Net, Native AOT 1,033 614 / 1,062 / 1,576 Nuxt (cluster) 424 209 / 408 / 519 TanStack Start (cluster) 389 201 / 389 / 487 Next.js (cluster) 349 179 / 330 / 445 Laravel 81 56 / 79 / 157 .NET ran the calculation about three times faster than Node.js and fifteen times faster than PHP. It also used extra cores in one process without any extra code. Laravel gains cores by running more PHP workers. Node.js runs one request's JavaScript at a time, so a single Node.js server uses about one core. To give Next.js, TanStack Start and Nuxt the best chance on heavy work, their numbers here come from cluster mode: one server process per core, sharing one port, as PM2's cluster mode does. Run as a single process, like everywhere else on this page, they handled 207 (Next.js), 227 (TanStack Start) and 240 (Nuxt) requests per second. More cores didn't help. Cluster mode also roughly doubles their memory, since every process loads the whole app. Their cluster numbers come from a separate run on a different machine. Inertia.Net with its caching turned on All the results above run each setup without page caching. The dashboard data is still cached as described earlier. The results measure the complete request path, not only the framework or adapter. A real app usually caches what it can. So we ran the .NET app once more, next to a copy of itself with Inertia.Net's optional caching features turned on: - The SSR render cache keeps the HTML of a server-rendered page. When the next visitor gets exactly the same page, Inertia.Net sends that HTML without asking Node to render it again. See Server-side rendering. - Two Node renderers instead of one, so rendering can use both CPU cores. - Cached props with stale-while-revalidate : the dashboard totals and each page of the todo list are kept in memory for a few seconds and refreshed in the background. See Props. Plain and tuned builds ran side by side on the same machines: Page, first visit JIT JIT, tuned Native AOT Native AOT, tuned --- ---: ---: ---: ---: Home 3,528 20,800 4,378 17,952 Todo list, 25 rows 1,561 25,756 3,293 23,443 Todo list, 100 rows 562 15,119 1,033 13,745 Dashboard 2,819 20,903 3,586 18,054 New todo form 7,068 56,746 7,773 49,923 With caching on, server-rendered pages were served 4 to 27 times faster, in about a millisecond, because a cached page skips rendering entirely. Form posts and the heavy calculation didn't change, since nothing there is cached. The second Node renderer adds about 25 MB of memory. The render cache uses the page's data as its key, so pages with per-user data make one entry per user. Turn the render cache on for pages that are the same for every visitor, such as landing, catalog and article pages. The other frameworks have caching of their own, so these numbers aren't in the tables above. The next section turns caching on for all of them. Every framework with its caching turned on Comparing a cached Inertia.Net with uncached rivals wouldn't be fair. So we gave every app its own framework's caching, set the same way. Pages are kept for 60 seconds and todo lists for 10. Each is served stale, which means the expired copy is still sent while a fresh copy is made in the background. Everything is kept in the app's memory. - Next.js: 'use cache' on the page components and their data. - TanStack Start and Nuxt: Nitro route rules, which store the whole response. - Laravel: the popular spatie/laravel-responsecache package, which also stores the whole response. Requests per second for a first visit, every app with caching on: Page, first visit Inertia.Net Inertia.Net (AOT) Nuxt TanStack Start Laravel Next.js --- ---: ---: ---: ---: ---: ---: Home 55,711 50,970 18,471 12,997 1,177 558 Todo list, 25 rows 34,020 32,889 15,481 9,543 1,201 439 Todo list, 100 rows 22,834 20,007 6,835 3,882 868 201 Dashboard 55,439 50,105 18,151 11,680 1,206 424 New todo form 57,611 51,266 18,603 12,129 1,180 504 - Inertia.Net served 2 to 3 times more than Nuxt and 3 to 6 times more than TanStack Start , the next fastest. It did so while still running your code and loading fresh page data on every request, which the Nuxt, TanStack Start and Laravel caches skip. - Nuxt and TanStack Start gained the most from caching among the JavaScript frameworks, up to 15 times for Nuxt. - Laravel got 2 to 5 times faster but stopped near 1,200 requests per second, because every request still goes through its session and security layers. - Next.js didn't get faster. Its cache stores the output of components, but a page that reads the address bar, like the todo list, is still turned into HTML on every request. Next.js only serves ready-made HTML for pages that never change per request. What Inertia.Net caches, and what it doesn't Inertia.Net has two caches that work together, and you choose what goes in each. The SSR render cache stores HTML, not data. On a first visit Inertia.Net still runs your endpoint and builds the page's data as usual. It then looks up that exact data. If the same page with the same data was rendered recently, Inertia.Net sends the stored HTML and Node isn't called at all. Rendering with Node is the most expensive step of a server-rendered page, so this is where most of the speed comes from. Because the lookup uses the data itself, the cache can never show an out-of-date page. When one todo changes, the data changes, and the page is rendered fresh. Cached props store data. Add .Cache(key, duration) to a prop and Inertia.Net keeps its value, in memory or in Redis. The database isn't asked again until the value expires. With staleFor , an expired value is still served while a fresh one loads in the background. This is the only place Inertia.Net will show data that is a little old, and only for the props you mark. In the benchmark's tuned app, a todo list visit therefore reads the rows from the prop cache, finds the HTML in the render cache, and sends it. All of this takes well under a millisecond on the server. Moving between pages in the browser fetches only data and never involves Node, so for those requests the prop cache does the work. This is different from the other frameworks' caches, which store the whole response under its address. Those caches skip your code entirely on a hit. But they show the same response, possibly out of date, until it expires. They also need care so that one user's page isn't served to another. Inertia.Net always runs your code, so permissions and per-user data are checked on every request, and you decide which data may be a little old. See Server-side rendering for the render cache and Props for cached props. What this means for you - Pick the framework your team enjoys and knows. All five are fast enough for most apps at normal traffic. - Choose ASP.NET Core with Inertia.Net if C and the .NET backend ecosystem suit your team and you want React, Vue or Svelte pages without a separate page API. Treat the measured headroom as a result of this setup, not a speed boost promised by the adapter. - Choose Native AOT for the smallest memory, image and startup time, if plain Npgsql or Dapper-style data access suits you. - Choose TanStack Start for a light, type-safe React stack in TypeScript end to end. - Choose Next.js for the largest React ecosystem, static and incrementally generated content, or Vercel's platform. - Choose Nuxt if your team writes Vue and wants conventions that remove a lot of setup. - Choose Laravel for PHP's most productive ecosystem and everything built in. These come from one run on shared cloud machines, with the load generator running next to the apps. Different routes ran on different machines, so compare apps within a table, not one table with another. Measure your own app on your own hardware before you rely on any of them. Run it yourself The app code, the run script and every setting are in benchmarks/frameworks. Its README explains how to run the comparison on your own machine or on GitHub Actions and lists the caveats. Every route in both modes, with latency percentiles and fixed-rate runs, is in the full results. The run with caching turned on is in its own results file. For what Inertia.Net itself costs next to a plain Minimal API, see Performance.

title: Infinite scroll
description: Merge pages of items and report paging metadata to the InfiniteScroll client component.
body: Use infinite scroll when a reader should see more items as they reach the end of a list. Scroll(...) merges the items inside a value and reports paging metadata to the client component. The items sit in the wrapper , which is "data" by default. See Pagination for numbered and cursor pages, query binding and data-source delegates. The client Metadata ScrollMetadata(PageName, PreviousPage, NextPage, CurrentPage) is a record. Page values can be int , long , string or null . Cursor paging uses strings. Metadata comes from the metadata: argument, or from the value if it implements IProvidesScrollMetadata . Without either, the render throws an exception with a message that names the prop. The client sends X-Inertia-Infinite-Scroll-Merge-Intent: prepend when scrolling up. The wrapper is then reported under prependProps instead of mergeProps . scrollProps[path].reset is true when the request lists the path in X-Inertia-Reset . Combining with other props Scroll(...) accepts the five loader shapes. You can combine it with .Defer() , .Once() and .Rescue() : A deferred scroll prop reports "posts.data" in the same way as a resolved one. This behavior deliberately fixes an inertia-laravel quirk. Infinite scroll also limits the payload size. Load 10 to 20 items per page instead of sending an unbounded list on the first request.

title: Partial reloads
description: Reload only the props a page needs with only and except filters.
body: In a partial reload, the Inertia client reloads the current page and asks for a subset of its props. Deferred props, polling and infinite scroll work this way. You can also use a partial reload directly for dashboard refresh buttons and filters. To refresh props when something changes on the server, without polling, use live props. From the client router.visit('/users', { only: ['users'] }) works for a new page too. The client sends these headers: Header Meaning --- --- X-Inertia-Partial-Component The component being rendered X-Inertia-Partial-Data The only list X-Inertia-Partial-Except The except list Filtering applies only when the partial component equals the component being rendered. Server behavior - Paths are dot paths and match on a . boundary. only: ["user"] includes user.name . only: ["user.name"] includes user.name and keeps user as a container. - except takes priority over only . Always(...) ignores both. - The children of a value produced by a loader are not filtered. Nested literal InertiaProps are filtered. - Loaders of excluded props never run. - Selecting an array descendant ( rows.1.extra ) reloads the complete array, including sibling fields and nested loaders. A descendant except excludes the entire array. Always still wins. - Omitted or rescued direct array elements keep their positions as null . - A missing or empty list header means “no filter”, which differs from an empty list. Always(...) is sent even when a partial reload does not ask for it. Use it for props the page cannot render without. Do not use it for expensive data. What the client keeps A reloaded prop replaces the client's value by default. A prop resolved from a loader is sent in full. To combine values instead, use merge props. Deferred and once props Deferred props are loaded through partial reloads. X-Inertia-Partial-Data asks for the deferred group, and the server records which deferred props it has sent. Once props that the reload asks for always resolve. The client sends X-Inertia-Except-Once-Props with the keys it already holds, so the server can skip them while keeping the onceProps metadata. Testing partial reloads Inertia.Net.Testing replays the request with the right headers: ReloadOnlyAsync asserts that the requested prop is present. ReloadExceptAsync asserts that the excluded prop is missing.

title: Introduction
description: Inertia.Net is a .NET 10 and .NET 11 server adapter for Inertia.js v3. Build React, Vue and Svelte apps without a separate API.
body: Inertia.Net lets your C routes render React, Vue or Svelte pages. In each route, you choose a component and pass it the data it needs. Inertia calls that data props . Sign-in, validation and database queries live in your ASP.NET Core app. Your frontend framework handles what the user sees and interacts with. You can build and ship the server and frontend as one app. Start with a working todo app and try a C validation rule in the browser. First 10 minutes How it works The first request returns HTML with the page object embedded. The page object holds the component name and its props. Inertia links and form submissions request the next page in the background and swap the component while the browser keeps its state. Your .NET app still handles the request. The adapter adds the protocol middleware, prop resolution, redirect semantics, flash data and asset tags. What you get Minimal APIs, MVC controllers and FastEndpoints share the same core package and protocol behavior. Lazy, optional, deferred, merged, once, cached, rescued and infinite-scroll props. CSRF cookies, encrypted state, asset versioning, proxy support and SSR supervision. Props are written through System.Text.Json metadata. Inertia.Net does not use reflection over your page objects. Feature matrix Minimal API MVC controllers FastEndpoints --- :---: :---: :---: Package Inertia.Net Inertia.Net + Inertia.Net.Mvc Inertia.Net + Inertia.Net.FastEndpoints Render / Back / Location Render(...) returns IResult same, return IResult from an action Send.InertiaAsync(...) or return the result Validation redirect with errors .WithInertiaValidation() ModelState filter (global) c.ConfigureInertia() pre-processor Precognition .WithInertiaPrecognition() not available c.ConfigureInertia() Razor root view no ( app.html template) optional (tag helpers) no ( app.html template) Native AOT yes no (MVC itself is not AOT) yes (with the FastEndpoints source generator) The client packages are @inertiajs/react , @inertiajs/vue3 and @inertiajs/svelte , all version 3. Inertia.Net does not support v2 clients. This documentation site This site is an Inertia.Net app. The sidebar, search, docs pages and theme switcher are React components rendered by an ASP.NET Core Minimal API. Navigation uses Inertia links. The source is in docs/Inertia.Net.Docs , so the site is also a real example. Requirements - .NET 10 or .NET 11 SDK - JavaScript frontend build tools with npm, Bun, pnpm or Yarn. Managed SSR requires Node.js or Bun at runtime - An Inertia.js v3 client package for React, Vue or Svelte Use the starter template: dotnet new install Inertia.Net.Templates , then dotnet new inertia -n MyApp --framework react . It includes working pages, a form with validation, flash messages, CSRF and Vite configuration. Next steps - Why Inertia? explains what you get with C on the server and React, Vue or Svelte in the browser. - First 10 minutes takes you from the template to a working form you can change. - Install the packages in an existing app. - Follow the quick start for a minimal end-to-end setup. - Read the props reference when you are ready to model page data.

title: Deploying behind a proxy
description: Forwarded headers, secure cookies, compression, asset caching and multi-instance state.
body: Behind a load balancer or reverse proxy that terminates TLS, Kestrel sees plain HTTP unless the scheme is forwarded. When the scheme is not forwarded, the state and XSRF-TOKEN cookies are not marked Secure . Forwarded headers When the scheme cannot be forwarded, force the cookies to be secure: Multi-instance state When the app runs on several instances, share the Data Protection key ring, so that every instance can read the state cookie and antiforgery tokens: If you use the session store, sessions must be shared too, for example with Redis. The default cookie store only needs shared Data Protection keys. Keep the SSR server on loopback on each instance. See Server-side rendering. Compression Page JSON and HTML compress five to ten times. Compress at the proxy, or in the app: Over HTTPS, the middleware compresses only when you set o.EnableForHttps = true . Review BREACH for your pages first. Inertia.Net keeps the antiforgery token in a cookie, not in the body. However, a page that reflects request input next to a secret is still exposed. Asset caching Vite puts a content hash in every built file name, so files under build/assets can be cached as immutable: app.MapStaticAssets() does the same with build-time Brotli. Use it when the client is built before dotnet publish , so that the files are in wwwroot when the static web assets manifest is generated. Path base Call app.UsePathBase("/app") before UseInertia() . The page url , Vite URLs and Back() include the path base. If a proxy rewrites paths, set o.UrlResolver to return the URL that the browser sees. Health and readiness The SSR health check is covered in Server-side rendering. Deployment checklist - [ ] The client build script runs before dotnet publish ( npm run build , bun run build , pnpm run build or yarn run build ), or wwwroot/build is copied into the publish output. - [ ] app.html is copied to the publish output. - [ ] Forwarded headers are configured, or cookies are forced secure. - [ ] Data Protection keys are shared between instances. - [ ] Static assets under /build/assets are cached as immutable. - [ ] Response compression is enabled at the proxy or in the app. - [ ] SSR listens on loopback and its bundle is deployed when SSR is enabled. - [ ] The client build and server build are the same version, so X-Inertia-Version converges. Hosts and SSR failures Keep AllowedHosts configured. Ssr.ConnectTimeout limits the time to establish a connection. The default is five seconds. In SsrMode.Required , the exception message is generic. Diagnostic properties may contain private renderer details and should stay in trusted logs. Check published frontend assets Add a readiness check for the Vite entry keys used by your root view. Register it for production after building the frontend. The first probe checks the local build directory for the entry and the files reachable through both static and dynamic imports. An unhealthy result identifies a missing manifest key or file. The result is kept for the lifetime of the host, so publish assets before starting it and restart after replacing them. Use mount: "admin" to check a named mount. For CDN deployments, run the check on the staged local files before uploading them. The starter template includes the hidden manifest in publish output. If an existing project omits it, add this to its project file and build the frontend before publishing:

title: Flash data
description: Carry a one-time message, toast or typed value across a redirect.
body: Flash data is a message or value for the next page, such as “Contact saved.” Unlike shared props, it is not kept in browser history. Inertia.Net carries flash data across the redirect and any further redirects. The next response that is not a redirect consumes it. Flash data appears as page.flash , and only when there is some. On the client, read flash data from the page's flash or from the onFlash visit callback. The page's flash is usePage().flash , or page.flash in Svelte: The TypeScript generator can type page.flash . FlashData () takes the whole flash object. For the toast above, use record Flash(Toast? Toast) and call o.TypeScript.FlashData () . See TypeScript types. Inertia forms keep their input on the client after Back().WithErrors(...) . They do not need a WithInput() helper. For a full-page form submission, choose only safe fields to flash before redirecting: On the next page, read flash.old from the page and use the email to refill the field. Never flash passwords, tokens or other secrets. Remove a flash value In a handler, call http.Inertia().ForgetFlashed("toast", "user.name") before rendering or redirecting. This removes values set in this request or restored from a previous one. An exact key such as "user.name" wins over the nested path. If no flash values remain, the page has no flash field. The remaining values still expire normally. Where state is kept Some state must survive a redirect: flash data, errors, clearHistory and preserveFragment . When a request sets any of these and ends in a redirect, Inertia.Net saves the state in an IInertiaStateStore . The same applies when the request ends in a Location() / fragment 409 . Inertia.Net loads the state at the start of the next request. If the next request redirects again, the state is carried on, so Back() to a URL that itself redirects still shows the flash. Otherwise the response of the next request consumes the state. The state is also kept when the response is the version-mismatch 409 . Encrypted cookie (default) The default store is an encrypted cookie named .Inertia.State . The cookie is protected with ASP.NET Core Data Protection, and it is HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax . The store works without sessions and under Native AOT. Tampered or undecryptable cookies are ignored and deleted. The store logs a warning when the cookie is larger than about 4 KB, because browsers drop larger cookies. Session store Use the session store when flash data can be large or must not reach the browser, and you already run sessions. MVC TempData store This store keeps the state in MVC TempData, so the state follows your TempData provider. The provider is the default cookie provider, or AddSessionStateTempDataProvider() with AddSession() and app.UseSession() before app.UseInertia() . The store works for Minimal API endpoints too, because it saves TempData itself. It is not compatible with Native AOT. Your own store Implement IInertiaStateStore and register it before AddInertia : The methods move opaque bytes. The format belongs to Inertia.Net. Choosing a store Store Use when --- --- Encrypted cookie Default. Stateless, AOT safe, about 4 KB limit. Session Flash data can be large or must not reach the browser, and sessions already exist. TempData The app standardizes on MVC TempData, or you want to switch providers without changing code. Custom You need a shared store across instances or a different transport. In a multi-instance deployment, configure Data Protection with a shared key ring. Otherwise the cookie written by one instance cannot be read by another. History flags encryptHistory is written only when set and is not carried across redirects. clearHistory and preserveFragment go through the state store. They apply to the next page rendered after the redirects, and are then consumed. See Redirects and history.

title: Page records
description: Optional typed page props that name their component once, generate their TypeScript type, and can hold the handler that renders them.
headings: Handle the request in the page record
body: A page record is a record that lists the props of a page, names its component once, and becomes the TypeScript type of the page. It is an opt-in alternative: use it when you want the props typed end to end. Render("Users/Index", new InertiaProps { ... }) is the default way to render a page, and it stays fully supported. See Pages and responses. You can mix both styles in one app, page by page. Declare a page record A record that implements IInertiaPage names its component once, so neither Render nor the TypeScript registration repeats it: A source generator writes AddGeneratedPages() , so it needs no reflection and works under Native AOT. PagesFrom(assembly) does the same with reflection. Use it for page records in another assembly. See TypeScript types for the generated file. A property can hold any prop factory. Give an InertiaProp its type with InertiaPropType so the TypeScript declaration is not unknown : Every host renders a page record the same way: Handle the request in the page record IInertiaPage only names the component. The library never calls into the record. A record can have static methods, so you can still keep the GET handler next to the props it fills, and map the method itself as the endpoint. The method's parameters bind like the parameters of any Minimal API handler: route values, query strings, services, ClaimsPrincipal and CancellationToken . A handler can be async and return another result when there is no page to show: Method groups go through the Request Delegate Generator like lambdas do, so a handler on a page record works under Native AOT. Keep POST , PUT and DELETE handlers with the rest of their feature, not on the record. These handlers validate input and redirect, so they do not render this page. Where the route lives The route pattern and its name stay on the endpoint ( MapGet(...).WithName(...) ), not on the record. More than one endpoint often renders the same component, such as a form page shown by GET /users/create and by GET /users/{id}/edit . One endpoint can also render different components. Typed routes are generated from endpoint names, so a named endpoint gets its routes.ts function with either rendering style. Compile-time component checks The Inertia.Net package includes an analyzer with these rules: Rule Reports --- --- INERTIA001 Two page records that claim one component. INERTIA002 A component name, in Render("...") , MapInertia or a page record, that has no page file under $(InertiaPagesDirectory) . INERTIA002 runs when the project file sets the pages directory:

title: Shared data
description: Share props with every page, statically or per request, and control the shared prop key list.
body: Shared props are merged into every page. Use them for values that every page needs and that are cheap to compute. When a page prop has the same key as a shared prop, the page prop wins. Register shared values Share values from anywhere with an HttpContext , such as middleware or a handler: The value can be any prop, including another factory: plans is resolved once, and the client keeps it across visits. context.Inertia().FlushShared() clears configured and request shared props for the current request only. It does not change application defaults or other requests. Validation errors remain available. Call Share(...) afterwards to add replacement request shares. To omit shared data on error pages only, set InertiaErrorPagesOptions.IncludeSharedProps = false . The shared prop key list The top-level shared keys are listed in the page object so the client can keep them across navigations: errors is always shared, so the list always contains at least "errors" . Turn the list off with: When to use shared props Use shared props for values that every page needs and that are cheap to compute: - the signed-in user or tenant name - the application name and locale - feature flags - a once-per-client value such as a plan catalogue Keep large or page-specific data in page props. Shared props are considered on every page response, including partial reloads, so keep them cheap or wrap an expensive value in Once . Wrapping a shared value in Once is the equivalent of Laravel's shareOnce . The client keeps the value across visits and sends X-Inertia-Except-Once-Props . The loader does not run again until the value expires. TypeScript The generated declarations infer shared props from the values passed to o.Share(...) . Factories and per-request shares are typed as unknown . Use o.TypeScript.SharedProps () when you want an explicit shape. See TypeScript types.

title: Authentication and rate limiting
description: Redirect Inertia visits to the login page, send rate-limited forms back with a flash message, and start from the --auth template.
body: Use UseInertiaRedirects() to redirect Inertia visits to the login page, and InertiaRateLimiting.OnRejected() to send rate-limited forms back with a flash message. The dotnet new inertia --auth template creates an app with both. Cookie sign-in The cookie handler answers an Inertia visit with 401, because the client sends X-Requested-With . Call UseInertiaRedirects() so that Inertia visits are redirected to the login page like browser requests. The redirect is a 303 after a POST , PUT , PATCH or DELETE . fetch calls and Precognition validation keep their 401. When access is denied, the 403 error page renders if AddInertiaErrorPages() handles 403. Otherwise the request is redirected to AccessDeniedPath . See Error pages for the 403 and 429 pages. Rate limiting InertiaRateLimiting.OnRejected() answers a rejected request the way the client expects: - An Inertia form submission is redirected back with a flash message ( flash.error by default) and Retry-After . - A Precognition request gets 429 with Precognition: true . - Anything else gets 429. When AddInertiaErrorPages() handles 429, Inertia requests get the error page instead. Call UseRateLimiter() after UseInertia() , so the flash message of a rejected submission is saved. Start from the template dotnet new inertia --auth creates an app with both: - A /login page whose form checks fields with Precognition. The demo sign-in is demo@example.com / password, accepted only in Development. - A protected /dashboard , and logout. - The signed-in user shared as auth.user . - A sign-in rate limit that sends the form back with a flash message. - Inertia visits to a protected page are redirected to the login page ( UseInertiaRedirects() ). Signing in returns to the page that asked for it ( ReturnUrl , local paths only). The cookie handler sends signed-out visitors to /login?ReturnUrl=/the/page , and the login form posts the value back. Replace the in-memory UserStore with ASP.NET Core Identity or your user database.

title: Performance
description: Memory, requests per second and CPU with and without Inertia, hosting guidance, payload limits and the design choices behind the adapter.
headings: Make rendering faster: register your JSON context first
body: The benchmarks cover page rendering, partial reloads, deferred props, SSR, caching and state storage. They are controlled microbenchmarks, not estimates of production throughput. To compare a whole app with Next.js, TanStack Start, Nuxt and Laravel, see Framework comparison. With and without Inertia This section measures what Inertia.Net costs next to a Minimal API without it. tests/Inertia.Net.HostingProbe serves the same screen both ways: a list of 25 users plus appName and auth , about 2.7 KB of JSON. - Plain JSON API returns the data from Results.Json . - Plain HTML shell writes it into a hand-made HTML page. - Inertia visit is the X-Inertia JSON response. - Inertia first load is the HTML page the browser gets on the first request. Each row runs in its own process, under load from 64 keep-alive connections. The first four handlers do no I/O, so the gap between them is the whole cost of the adapter. The two todo rows add a real handler: cookie sign-in and a SQLite query. All runs were on a GitHub-hosted ubuntu-24.04 runner (AMD EPYC 9V74, 4 vCPUs) on .NET 10. The server was pinned to 2 vCPUs and the load client to the other 2. Values are medians of 5 rounds, which agreed within about 2%. In the table, p99 is the response time that 99% of requests stay under, and RSS (resident set size) is the physical memory the process holds. Build (server GC) Scenario Req/s p99 Server CPU per request RSS at rest Peak RSS under load Startup --- --- ---: ---: ---: ---: ---: ---: JIT Plain JSON API 73,148 2.00 ms 27 µs 61 MB 77 MB 173 ms JIT Plain HTML shell 64,129 2.34 ms 30 µs 61 MB 78 MB 165 ms JIT Inertia visit (JSON) 57,241 2.32 ms 35 µs 74 MB 96 MB 217 ms JIT Inertia first load (HTML) 56,117 2.31 ms 35 µs 75 MB 92 MB 223 ms Native AOT Plain JSON API 65,364 2.28 ms 30 µs 29 MB 35 MB 28 ms Native AOT Plain HTML shell 55,776 2.19 ms 35 µs 29 MB 42 MB 28 ms Native AOT Inertia visit (JSON) 44,979 2.92 ms 44 µs 33 MB 48 MB 37 ms Native AOT Inertia first load (HTML) 44,666 2.97 ms 44 µs 33 MB 48 MB 35 ms JIT Todo app visit: EF Core + SQLite + cookie auth 4,411 38.88 ms 446 µs 115 MB 144 MB 786 ms Native AOT Todo app visit: Microsoft.Data.Sqlite + cookie auth 9,387 11.92 ms 206 µs 37 MB 50 MB 46 ms What this means for an app: - Memory. Compared with the plain apps, the Inertia rows use about 13 MB more at rest and 14–19 MB more at peak under load on JIT. On Native AOT they use about 4 MB more at rest and 6–13 MB more at peak. Almost all of the difference at rest comes from ASP.NET Core Data Protection. AddInertia registers it for its state cookie. Adding only AddDataProtection() to a plain app increased memory use by 12 MB on JIT and 5 MB on Native AOT. Inertia.Net itself uses about 1 MB at rest. An app with cookie sign-in, antiforgery or sessions already loads Data Protection. - CPU. An Inertia response costs 5–8 µs more server CPU than a hand-written JSON or HTML endpoint on JIT, and 9–14 µs more on Native AOT. On these do-nothing handlers that is 12–31% fewer requests per second. A handler that spends 1 ms on a database query loses under 1.5%. - A real handler. The todo rows read the signed-in user's 25 todos from SQLite on every request. The database work, not Inertia, sets their cost: 206–446 µs of CPU per request, against Inertia's 34–44 µs in total. On JIT the EF Core build serves 4,411 requests per second. The Native AOT build, which uses Microsoft.Data.Sqlite directly, serves 9,387. - Latency. Under 64 concurrent connections, p99 stays below 3 ms in every build without a database. - JIT or Native AOT. Native AOT uses about half the memory and starts six times faster. JIT serves more requests per second, because dynamic PGO keeps optimizing the hot path after startup. - GC mode. Workstation GC gave about the same throughput. Its RSS at rest was the same on JIT and up to 2 MB higher on Native AOT, and its peak under load was 2–14 MB higher. That is why the table uses server GC, the ASP.NET Core default. Run it yourself on Linux. It needs taskset , plus clang and zlib for the Native AOT build: The hosting-probe workflow runs the same probe on a GitHub runner whenever the probe changes, or on demand. The full table, including workstation GC and RSS after load, is in its job summary and in the benchmark results. Measure on a quiet machine. On a shared machine, other processes take CPU from both the server and the client, so requests per second varies from run to run. Memory and hosting For capacity planning, the useful number is how much memory the whole process needs at rest and under load, not a microbenchmark. These are reference points for complete apps, measured on Linux x64 after the first request. They are not guarantees: App shape RSS at rest Peak RSS under load Plan for --- ---: ---: ---: Inertia.Net JIT app, no database ( samples/MinimalApi.React ) about 90 MB not measured 256–512 MB Inertia.Net Native AOT app ( tests/Inertia.Net.AotSmoke ) about 42 MB not measured 128–256 MB Small JIT todo app: EF Core + SQLite + cookie auth 115–117 MB 144–158 MB 256–512 MB Small Native AOT todo app: Microsoft.Data.Sqlite + source-generated JSON + cookie auth 37–39 MB 50–58 MB 128–256 MB Managed SSR process, small React app (Bun) +58 MB +99–106 MB add 128 MB Managed SSR process, small React app (Node) +89 MB +138–147 MB add 192 MB Managed SSR process, large app: this docs site, 3 MB bundle (Bun) +83 MB +324–344 MB add 384 MB Managed SSR process, large app: this docs site (Node) +138 MB +242–247 MB add 320 MB All rows were measured on Linux x64 after the first request. The rows below the first two come from the hosting probes: - Todo apps. These are the probe's todo mode: a signed-in user's 25 todos, read from SQLite on every request, as an Inertia visit. Both rows cover 64 concurrent connections under server and workstation GC on the GitHub runner. The Native AOT build uses Microsoft.Data.Sqlite directly, because EF Core's runtime query compilation is not Native AOT compatible. - SSR rows. These are the Bun or Node process that managed SSR starts, measured with eng/ssr-memory-probe.sh . The script renders each page once ("at rest"), then sends 3,000 renders from 8 parallel clients ("peak"). The small app is samples/MinimalApi.React . The large app is this site's MDX bundle. A few things to plan for: - SSR peaks. Bun starts smaller, but the large bundle peaked higher under Bun than under Node. Bun handed most of it back within seconds (144–222 MB 3 s later). Node kept its peak (229–239 MB). Size the SSR container for the peak. Runtime flags passed through n.Arguments barely change the peak: Bun's --smol peaked at 319–322 MB and Node's --max-old-space-size=128 at 228–230 MB, and both rendered about 2–4× slower. Measure your own bundle with eng/ssr-memory-probe.sh . - Bigger apps. PostgreSQL or MongoDB, image processing and a large cache move every number upward, so measure your own app under realistic concurrency. - Native AOT. It removes most JIT and reflection overhead, but it does not make EF Core or a database free. For containers: - Set a memory limit for the container instead of relying on the host. .NET uses this limit to size its heap. - Keep the default server GC with dynamic adaptation (DATAS). DATAS has been on by default since .NET 9. In the hosting probe, turning it off ( DOTNET GCDynamicAdaptationMode=0 ) raised peak memory from 84 MB to 126 MB on JIT and from 47 MB to 122 MB on Native AOT. - Leave headroom for the GC, the OS page cache and request bursts. - Expect SSR to add a second process. If the Bun renderer is optional, SsrMode.Preferred lets the app fall back to client rendering when the renderer is unavailable. - Profile with real page sizes. A dashboard with deferred props and a paginated feed behaves very differently from a page that serializes every row. For in-process render throughput and allocations, use the benchmark project: Targeted probes: --render-probe , --ssr-probe , --mvc-probe , --payload-probe and --cache-probe . Make rendering faster: register your JSON context first Inertia.Net uses System.Text.Json to write props as JSON. If your app has a source-generated JsonSerializerContext , register it first in TypeInfoResolverChain . Inertia.Net then uses the generated code for plain values (records, lists of records, strings, numbers) instead of System.Text.Json's general-purpose path. In the hosting probe, this reduced CPU work per Inertia request by about 16% on JIT and 20% on Native AOT. dotnet new inertia already does this. In your own app: Inertia.Net uses the generated code only when the output would be exactly the same. It checks this for you and falls back to System.Text.Json's general-purpose path when: - the context is not first in TypeInfoResolverChain - its settings differ from your app's JSON options (for example, omitting JsonSerializerDefaults.Web gives PascalCase instead of camelCase names) - your JSON options have custom converters, or PreserveBigIntegers is on - a type has a property name with characters other than letters, digits, , - , . and $ Payload size Inertia.Net builds the whole page in memory before sending the first byte. A loader failure therefore never leaves a half-written 200 response. Each active request keeps its whole page in memory while sending it. The server sends Inertia (JSON) responses in 32 KB pieces, so its send buffers do not hold a second full copy of a large page. Buffers for pages under 1 MB are reused between requests. Larger ones are freed after the response, so one unusually large page does not keep that memory reserved for the life of the app. Keep pages well under a megabyte: - paginate with Scroll - defer slow data with Defer - load on demand with Optional - use a partial reload for refresh buttons and filters Ssr.MaxPageBytes keeps larger pages off the SSR server, and Ssr.MaxResponseBytes limits the size of the SSR server's answer. Neither setting limits the props. Design notes - Single pass. One recursive walk filters props, runs loaders, writes JSON to a Utf8JsonWriter and collects the metadata. There is no intermediate object tree. - Pooled buffers. The page is written to a pooled IBufferWriter , and the path tracker is a pooled char[] . A path becomes a string only when metadata needs it. - Version check before the handler. A stale client costs one header comparison and a 409 . - No per-request mutable singletons. Per-request state lives in an InertiaFeature on HttpContext.Features , so concurrent requests cannot leak history or flash settings into one another. - Plain DTOs take the fast path. Inertia.Net checks whether a POCO, list or typed dictionary can hold InertiaProp values ( InertiaProp , object or dictionary members/elements). It caches this result per type and checks the contents for props only for those types. Everything else uses one Serialize call, through your generated JSON context when it writes the same output. An object whose object members hold only plain values at render time (no InertiaProp , dictionary, JsonElement or JsonNode ) is also serialized in one call, unless a partial reload filters inside it. - UTF-8 throughout. SSR output and the MVC tag helpers write UTF-8 bytes. Nothing large is turned into a .NET string. - Cached assets. The Vite manifest is parsed once, the root template is parsed once into pre-encoded UTF-8 segments, and the production tags are pre-rendered per entry set and path base. The version is a precomputed string compared ordinally. A missing manifest, template or SSR bundle is re-checked at most once per second. - Sync loaders stay sync. Func loaders are not wrapped in closures. Most per-request allocation in a real handler is the props you build, not the render. Paired render measurements Warm, in-process probes on .NET 10 compared 32 alternating rounds in two runs. Times are medians of within-round ratios. B/op (bytes allocated per operation) values are from run 2. Workload Before B/op After B/op Run 1 paired time Run 2 paired time --- ---: ---: ---: ---: JSON, 20 mixed props 1,736 1,736 −1.6% −0.6% Integer-key dictionary, 1,000 props 176,592 166,688 −52.2% −53.7% GUID-key dictionary, 500 rows 140,712 140,304 −28.5% −33.0% Eight scroll props, append wrappers 6,664 6,088 −2.2% −3.4% Eight scroll props, prepend wrappers 6,880 6,112 −6.2% −5.4% These synthetic measurements do not establish HTTP throughput or general latency. Pooled entries grow from 24 to 32 bytes, so warm savings do not imply a smaller cold or concurrent pool footprint. Full methods, controls and rejected candidates are in benchmark results. Parallel prop planning and DevTools recording each use a process-wide latch that remains active after first use. Measure with the features used by your own app.

title: Asset versioning
description: Tell the client when its JavaScript and CSS are stale, and reload once when they are.
body: The asset version tells the client when its JavaScript and CSS are stale, so that the client can perform a full page reload. The server resolves the asset version in this order: 1. InertiaOptions.VersionResolver(HttpContext) , when it returns non-null; 2. else InertiaOptions.Version ; 3. else a hash of the Vite manifest (the first 16 bytes of its SHA-256, in hex), computed once and recomputed in Development when the file changes; 4. else "" . How the client checks it When an Inertia GET carries a different X-Inertia-Version , the server answers 409 . The response carries X-Inertia-Location (the request's path and query) and X-Inertia-Version . The client then performs a full page reload. The check runs before your handler , so no work is wasted rendering a page that will be discarded. Other methods never get this 409 . Choosing a version - Vite manifest hash (default). Nothing to configure. A new build changes the manifest and the version. - Assembly version or build id. Use it when the client build is not tied to the manifest, or when several apps share assets. - Per-request version. Use it for multi-tenant apps with different frontend builds per tenant. A VersionResolver that returns a random value on every call makes the client reload forever. Different instances behind a load balancer must serve the same build, or the client will bounce between versions. Path base X-Inertia-Location holds the path base, the path and the query of the request. It has no scheme or host, so the client resolves it against the page it is on, and a reverse proxy cannot make it wrong. Other features still need forwarded headers behind a proxy. See Deploying.
